ACAD.name: Acadia National Park
ACAD.summary: Acadia National Park was established in 1919 as Lafayette National Park — the first national park east of the Mississippi River — and renamed Acadia in 1929. Located on Mount Desert Island and surrounding areas along the Maine coast, the park protects roughly 49,000 acres of granite-peaked mountains, rocky shoreline, woodlands, and glacially carved lakes. George B. Dorr and Charles W. Eliot led the private land conservation effort that made the park possible, with John D. Rockefeller Jr. later financing the construction of 45 miles of carriage roads. The park's diverse ecosystems mark the overlap of northern boreal and eastern deciduous forests, supporting over 1,100 plant species and serving as a critical stopover for migratory birds along the Atlantic Flyway.

AMIS.name: Amistad National Recreation Area
AMIS.summary: Amistad National Recreation Area was authorized by Congress in 1965 and established in 1990 along the U.S.–Mexico border near Del Rio, Texas. The recreation area surrounds Amistad Reservoir, a 64,860-acre international lake formed by the Amistad Dam on the Rio Grande, built jointly by the United States and Mexico. The region contains some of the oldest and best-preserved rock art in North America, with over 200 known pictograph sites created by hunter-gatherer peoples over a span of roughly 4,000 years. The Fate Bell Shelter and Panther Cave are among the most significant archaeological sites in the Lower Pecos Canyonlands.

ANDE.name: Andersonville NHS
ANDE.summary: Andersonville National Historic Site in southwestern Georgia preserves the site of Camp Sumter, the largest Confederate military prison during the Civil War. Operational from February 1864 to April 1865, the stockade held up to 32,000 Union prisoners of war in a space originally designed for 10,000, and nearly 13,000 died from disease, malnutrition, and exposure. The site was designated a national historic site in 1970 and also serves as home to the National Prisoner of War Museum, which honors all American prisoners of war throughout the nation's history. The adjacent Andersonville National Cemetery, established in 1865, remains an active national cemetery.

ANTI.name: Antietam National Battlefield
ANTI.summary: Antietam National Battlefield in Sharpsburg, Maryland, preserves the site of the Battle of Antietam, fought on September 17, 1862 — the bloodiest single day in American military history, with an estimated 23,000 casualties. The Union's strategic victory gave President Abraham Lincoln the political leverage to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later, fundamentally shifting the war's purpose to include the abolition of slavery. Established as a national battlefield site in 1890, the park encompasses approximately 3,230 acres of rolling farmland and includes landmarks such as Burnside Bridge, the Dunker Church, and Bloody Lane.

ARCH.name: Arches National Park
ARCH.summary: Arches National Park in eastern Utah protects over 2,000 natural stone arches — the densest concentration of such formations in the world — along with pinnacles, balanced rocks, and eroded sandstone fins. The landscape was shaped over 300 million years as salt deposits, sandstone layers, and erosion created the park's distinctive red-rock formations. Originally proclaimed a national monument by President Herbert Hoover in 1929, it was redesignated as a national park in 1971. Delicate Arch, the park's most iconic feature, has become a widely recognized symbol of Utah and appears on the state's license plates.

ARHO.summary:
Arlington House stands on a high ridge above the Potomac River, its massive portico facing Washington, D.C. George Washington Parke Custis, Martha Washington’s grandson, was raised by Martha and George Washington; when she died in 1802 he inherited 1,100 acres on the Potomac and the people she had enslaved. Between 1802 and 1818 enslaved workers and free labor built his house, modeled on a Greek temple, as the first memorial to George Washington and a museum for the family’s Washington heirlooms. [1] [2]

In 1831 his only surviving child, Mary Anna Randolph Custis, married Lt. Robert E. Lee in the family parlor. For thirty years the house was the Lees’ home and a working plantation where enslaved people numbered as many as 63 at one time. In April 1861 Lee resigned from the U.S. Army and sided with Virginia; Union troops occupied the heights, the Army built a Freedmen’s Village on the estate in 1863, and in 1864 it declared 200 acres a military cemetery — the beginning of Arlington National Cemetery. By August 1864, the Park Service’s 2015 foundation document says, more than two dozen soldiers had been buried within a few yards of the mansion to keep the Lee family from returning. [1] [2]

A 1925 joint resolution of Congress authorized restoring the mansion as a memorial to Lee; the Park Service took it over in 1933, and it was redesignated Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial in 1972. Only 19 of Custis’s original 1,100 acres lie within the memorial. The 2010 park brochure presents Lee as a figure of post-war reconciliation; the 2015 foundation document also names “Slavery and Freedom” as one of the park’s five interpretive themes and counts the two slave quarters among its fundamental resources. [5] [1] [2]

black.html: The war turned the estate into a refuge. In 1863 the Army founded Freedmen’s Village on roughly 400 acres in the south of the property for people who had escaped or been freed from slavery and come to Washington: it had homes, churches, a school and a hospital, and from 1866 to 1868 residents rented ten-acre parcels of the old estate to farm their way to independence. Quartermaster General Montgomery Meigs laid out the 200-acre cemetery so it would not interfere with the village, but wanted soldiers buried nearer the mansion to prevent its future use as a residence. By January 1871 the cemetery’s records counted about 4,100 Black burials — 343 U.S. soldiers and 3,757 former slaves. Once the courts gave the United States clear title, the Army moved to remove civilians from the military reservation: according to the 2024 landscape inventory, the village’s 763 residents were evicted and it was disbanded around 1900 (the 2010 brochure says all were gone by 1890). [3] [4] [1]

slavery.html:
George Washington Parke Custis’s will freed the people he held in slavery no later than five years after his death, provided the estate was solvent. He died in 1857; Lee, as executor, managed more than 60 enslaved workers, and in December 1862 he was obliged to carry out the will. The 2010 park brochure quotes Lee calling slavery a moral and political evil while holding that only Providence should decide its fate. Household workers lived in twin quarters built to echo the mansion; Selina Gray, the head housekeeper, lived with her family in one room of the south quarters. [1]

In 1826 Custis gave Maria and Charles Syphax a 17-acre parcel on the estate’s southern edge, where a church for the enslaved community also stood; only in 1865 were they allowed to buy it legally. On March 3, 1930, two of Thornton and Selina Gray’s daughters, Annie Baker (77) and Ada Thompson (73), toured the house with architect L. M. Leisenring and described how its rooms had been used. [3] [4]

women.html: After her father’s death in 1857 Arlington was legally owned by Mary Anna Custis Lee, though her husband became its master. From her mother’s death in 1853 she managed the household and its enslaved workers despite worsening rheumatoid arthritis; she and her daughters grew roses in the flower garden and sold them to help the American Colonization Society send freed slaves to Liberia. When she left in May 1861 she handed her keys to Selina Gray, who guarded the family’s possessions; by January 1862 Gray found that boxes of Mount Vernon relics had been broken into and reported the theft to General McDowell. In 1864 the government took the estate when Mrs. Lee could not appear in person to pay its taxes. Visiting shortly before her death in 1873, she wrote that it seemed but a dream of the past. [3] [1] [4]

BICY.name: Big Cypress National Preserve

photos.caption: A cypress swamp in Big Cypress National Preserve
photos.note: On-page caption: "Cypress swamps while appearing mysterious, are peaceful and serene." credit "NPS Photo". Resized from 5168x3448.

BICY.summary:
Water is the unifying force of Big Cypress: its 729,000 acres of largely freshwater wetland connect five habitats — hardwood hammocks, pinelands, prairies, cypress swamps and estuaries — and the preserve protects the flow of fresh water into the estuaries of Everglades National Park and the Ten Thousand Islands. By some accounts its watershed supplies more than half the surface water that reaches the Everglades from outside them. The preserve holds the largest dwarf cypress forests in North America and the largest old-growth South Florida slash pine forest, the ghost orchid, one of more than 30 native orchids, and the heart of the primary range of the Florida panther, one of the most endangered mammals in the world. [1] [2] [3]

In 1968 construction began on what was meant to be the world’s largest jetport, which would have devastated the natural flow of fresh water through the swamp. A coalition of conservationists, hunters, landowners and Seminole and Miccosukee people stopped it, and on October 11, 1974, President Gerald Ford signed the law creating Big Cypress as one of the nation’s first national preserves — a new kind of park where hunting, off-road vehicles, oil and gas extraction, private land and the customary uses of the Miccosukee and Seminole would continue alongside protection. Congress enlarged it by 147,000 acres in 1988. The land carries evidence of some 15,000 years of human use. [1] [2] [3]

black.html: Black workers helped cut the cypress forest of Big Cypress. A 2002 study prepared for the preserve by Frank and Audrey Peterman found that the railroad workers and Tamiami Trail builders who made the logging possible were overwhelmingly Black, and that the logging and sawmill labor pool was predominantly Black. Spurred in part by World War II’s need for durable timber, the Lee Tidewater Cypress Company alone shipped about 360 million board feet of cypress from 1944 to 1956. Copeland, a Lee Tidewater company town, had a Black side and a White side; the C. J. Jones company paid its workers in company scrip, good for rent and goods at its store, while Lee Tidewater paid in dollars. Frances Hodge, who in her 2002 interview said she came to Copeland in 1950 and who cooked at the company boardinghouse, serving white workers, for 50 cents an hour, remembered so much work that people slept on others’ porches — until the power saw came and the jobs were gone. The authors note how rarely the local papers of the day even mentioned these workers. [4]

sources.title: Frank & Audrey Peterman, African Americans and the Sawmills of Big Cypress — A Brief History (Earthwise Productions for NPS, Big Cypress National Preserve, 2002)

climate.html: The preserve’s 2016 foundation document records the change already under way: average annual temperature has risen at a statistically significant rate since 1950, sea levels and storm-surge heights have risen, and the preserve has been in or near 19 hurricane-strength storms over the past century. Rising seas and storm surge threaten loss of land and habitat, rising groundwater and saltwater intrusion into freshwater ecosystems, and an imbalance between salt and fresh water that can favor invasive species. The Gulf Coast region is already showing an enhanced hydrological cycle — more intense rain, stronger storms — and the preserve’s shallow waters are expected to track the warming closely. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Big Cypress National Preserve (2016) — FRV analyses and key issues on climate change

indigenous.html: The swamp was a refuge as well as a home. The 2024 administrative history recounts how U.S. troops pursued Seminole warriors into the Everglades during the Second Seminole War, and how in the Third the United States sought to remove the remaining Seminole from Big Cypress and the Everglades. Abiaka, a Miccosukee medicine man also known as Sam Jones, led warriors who defeated Zachary Taylor’s forces at Lake Okeechobee in 1837 and refused to relocate to Indian Territory. When fighting ended in stalemate by 1858, many Seminole, Billy Bowlegs among them, agreed to go to Oklahoma, but about 150, Abiaka included, stayed in the traditional villages of Big Cypress, where he remained based until his death in 1866. The Seminole population of Big Cypress grew through the late nineteenth century, and the Big Cypress Seminole Reservation now borders the preserve to the north. [3] In creating the preserve, Congress honored the customs and occupancy of the Miccosukee and Seminole peoples, whose villages stand in it today as they have for generations. [1]

sources.title: A Question of Balance (NPS administrative history, 2024), ch. 1, Prehistoric and Historic Background, pp. 9–11

women.html: Marjory Stoneman Douglas is remembered for saving the Everglades, but her newly formed Friends of the Everglades also played a major role in the coalition that turned back the jetport and won protection for Big Cypress, and her book The Everglades: River of Grass describes the swamp in detail. [1] [2] In the logging town of Copeland a generation earlier, Annie Mae Perry, a logger’s wife known far and wide as “Mother Perry,” served as midwife and delivered more than 500 babies in Copeland, Jerome, Immokalee, Everglades City and Naples; decades later she still gathered them every June. [4]

BISC.name: Biscayne National Park
BISC.summary: Biscayne National Park in southeastern Florida protects 172,971 acres of marine and coastal environments, making it one of the largest marine parks in the National Park System. Ninety-five percent of the park is water, encompassing Biscayne Bay, the northernmost Florida Keys, and a portion of the third-largest barrier reef in the world. Originally established as Biscayne National Monument in 1968 after a citizen-led campaign blocked a proposed industrial seaport, it was redesignated as a national park in 1980. The park preserves mangrove shorelines, the shallow waters of Biscayne Bay, the undeveloped upper Florida Keys, and living coral reefs supporting over 600 species of fish.

BLRI.name: Blue Ridge Parkway
BLRI.summary: The Blue Ridge Parkway stretches 469 miles along the crest of the Blue Ridge Mountains, connecting Shenandoah National Park in Virginia to Great Smoky Mountains National Park in North Carolina. Construction began in 1935 as a New Deal public works project and was not completed until 1987 with the opening of the Linn Cove Viaduct. Designed as a recreational motor road with no commercial vehicles allowed, the parkway passes through some of the oldest mountains in the world — the southern Appalachians — and features over 200 overlooks with sweeping views of the Blue Ridge. It is consistently the most-visited unit of the National Park System, drawing over 15 million recreational visitors annually.

BLSC.name: Blackwell School National Historic Site
BLSC.summary: Blackwell School National Historic Site in Marfa, Texas, was established on November 11, 2022, as the 423rd unit of the National Park System. The school operated from the 1880s through 1965 as the segregated school for Mexican American children in the Marfa Independent School District during the era of "Juan Crow" discrimination in Texas. Students were punished for speaking Spanish and faced systematic educational inequality. The site was championed by former students and their descendants — known as the Blackwell School Alliance — who preserved the remaining adobe classroom building and shared their oral histories to ensure this chapter of civil rights history would not be forgotten.

BRCA.name: Bryce Canyon National Park
BRCA.summary: Bryce Canyon National Park in southwestern Utah is renowned for its extraordinary collection of hoodoos — tall, thin spires of rock formed by frost weathering and stream erosion of the Claron Formation limestone. Despite its name, Bryce Canyon is not a true canyon but rather a series of natural amphitheaters carved into the eastern edge of the Paunsaugunt Plateau. The area was designated a national monument in 1923 and became a national park in 1928. The Paiute people, who inhabited the region for centuries before European contact, called the hoodoos "red rocks standing like men in a bowl-shaped canyon" in their oral tradition.

BUIS.name: Buck Island Reef National Monument
BUIS.summary: Buck Island Reef National Monument protects a small uninhabited island and its surrounding coral reef ecosystem located 1.5 miles off the northeast coast of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands. President John F. Kennedy established the monument in 1961, and it was expanded by President Bill Clinton in 2001 to encompass 19,015 acres of submerged lands. The monument's barrier reef — one of the finest in the Caribbean — includes an underwater snorkeling trail established by the National Park Service. The island itself supports dry tropical forest and serves as nesting habitat for endangered hawksbill and green sea turtles.

CACO.summary:
Cape Cod is a slender arm of sand and glacial debris curving some 60 miles into the Atlantic, one of the largest glacially formed peninsulas in the world. Wind and water never stop moving it: sand is torn from one stretch of shore and laid down on another, and the Great Beach on the ocean side is one of the longest uninterrupted sandy shorelines on the East Coast. Cape Cod National Seashore, authorized on August 7, 1961, protects about 44,000 acres along a 40-mile stretch between Chatham and Provincetown — beaches and dunes, kettle ponds, pine barrens, heathland and some 1,875 acres of salt marsh. [1] [1]

Archeological sites here record more than 9,000 years of human occupation, and by the 1600s the Wampanoag used or lived on all of the land now inside the seashore — use the Park Service says continues today. In 1620 the Cape was the Pilgrims’ first landfall and the place where they drafted the Mayflower Compact. Later Cape Codders took to whaling, fishing and shellfishing; lighthouses and lifesaving stations still line the outer shore; and the first transatlantic cable (1866) and the first exchange of transatlantic wireless messages (1903) went out from this coast. [1]

The Park Service’s own foundation document names what is at stake: the forces that shape the Cape are directly affected by climate change, and the seashore is a place to watch it happen. At the Marconi Station Site in Wellfleet, where the peninsula is only a mile wide, much of the high cliff has eroded since Guglielmo Marconi built his towers there in 1901. [1] [1]

climate.html:
The salt marshes are where rising seas show first. The 2018 foundation document finds evidence of sea-level rise in every one of the seashore’s salt marshes, which it says are getting wetter, and says their vegetation is changing rapidly in response. A 2020 Park Service study of marshes surveyed from 2003 to 2018 found both dominant marsh grasses (Spartina alterniflora and S. patens) declining, mostly from sea-level rise, crab grazing and wave erosion, and suggests that marsh migration is not keeping up with the losses; those marshes hold an estimated 18,000 metric tons of carbon. [1] [1]

On the ocean side, bluff erosion — a natural process the Park Service says is now being influenced by sea-level rise — has averaged 2.5 to 3 feet a year over a century, and the Nantucket tide gauge shows the sea rising faster here than the national average. Even the kettle ponds are warming: Gull Pond’s August surface water has grown warmer since 1980. [1] [1]

indigenous.html:
When Samuel de Champlain mapped Nauset Bay in 1605 he saw a harbor bordered by wigwams and recorded about 150 people living around it, farming and fishing. That was a late chapter: Paleo-Indian projectile points indicate that people have lived on, or at least crossed, this land for 10,000 years. The Park Service’s archeological survey, begun in 1979, found shellfish being gathered at least 4,000 years ago, some people living on the Outer Cape year-round in the late Woodland period, and a community in sustained contact with other Native peoples of the Northeast. A communal burial at Indian Neck in Wellfleet held more than two dozen people and dates to about A.D. 880–1155. [1] [1]

After 1620 Plymouth colonists came to Nauset to buy corn and trade, spreading diseases against which the Nauset had no immunity; their population fell drastically. In 1639 about half the English at Plymouth moved to the Nauset area and founded what is now Eastham. [1] [1]

CACR.summary:
A branch of the New World culture called Creole took root along the Cane River in 18th-century Louisiana, at what the Park Service calls the borderlands between New France and New Spain — a culture nurtured by French and Spanish colonial ways, steeped in Africanisms and enriched by American Indian contact. Cane River Creole National Historical Park preserves two of its plantations, Oakland and Magnolia, 10 and 20 miles south of Natchitoches: in the Park Service’s words the most intact French Creole cotton plantations in the United States, owned and worked by the same families, the Prud’hommes and the LeComte–Hertzogs, since the 18th century. Together they hold 70 historic structures, including eight rare brick slave quarters at Magnolia, and nearly 500,000 museum objects and archives. [n] [n]

Jean Baptiste Lecomte obtained the land grant that grew into Magnolia in 1753; Emmanuel Prud’homme received the grant at the core of Bermuda, later renamed Oakland, in 1789, and after the cotton gin’s invention in 1793 both families turned to cotton; enslaved workers built Prud’homme’s house in 1821. After the United States took possession of Louisiana in 1803, the park’s 2018 brochure explains, Anglo-American settlers poured in with their English language, Protestant religion and their own enslaved workers; life grew more constricted for non-whites as U.S. law removed colonial-era rights such as self-emancipation by purchase. [n]

Congress created the park on November 2, 1994, in the same law that created the 116,000-acre Cane River National Heritage Area — the only time a park unit and a heritage area have been legislated together. The Park Service says the park tells the story of oppressive plantation labor systems founded on slavery and replaced by tenant farming, sharecropping and day labor through the 1970s. [n]

black.html:
After the war a Union commander, on June 5, 1865, told freed people to stay on the premises to which they belonged, and Freedmen’s Bureau contracts at Bermuda paid six to ten dollars a month for men and five to eight for women. Those contracts, the park’s brochure says, differed from slavery mainly in requiring the worker’s consent; sharecropping ranged from a relatively benign feudalism to virtual bondage, the chains of slavery replaced by endless debt at the plantation store. Many stayed and rebuilt a community around church and family, often in the quarters that had housed their enslaved ancestors. [n] [n]

The first sharecropper did not leave Oakland until 1949. At Magnolia the Hertzogs housed day laborers in the brick cabins, which got electricity in the 1940s; mechanical pickers replaced the field crews in the 1960s, and the last residents, the Vercher family, moved out in the early 1970s. [n] [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)
NPSHistory.com: Cane River Creole NHP archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block

indigenous.html:
Before there was a French post at Natchitoches, this valley was Caddo country. By the end of the 1400s the Caddo numbered about 200,000, and the Red River valley was among the most densely settled parts of their homeland. Then came European disease and a years-long drought: archaeological evidence cited in the 2019 Historic Resource Study suggests the population fell by about 95 percent between 1500 and the 1680s. The Natchitoches confederacy, smallest of three, lived in villages on the river terraces between today’s Oakland Plantation and Natchitoches. [n]

In 1835 the Caddo sold all their lands by a treaty signed near Shreveport, for $30,000 in goods and horses and a promise of $50,000 over five years, pledging never to return to live as a nation within the United States. They went to Texas and later to Oklahoma, where the Caddo Nation is based today. Some stayed or returned, and the tribe still holds the Natchitoches area as its spiritual homeland. [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)

slavery.html:
Slavery built both plantations. Between 1810 and 1860 the Prud’hommes held between 50 and 145 people, placing them in the top nine percent of Louisiana slaveholders. The LeComtes held 234 people in 1860 across Magnolia and their other properties, 112 of them in the Magnolia quarters, completed in 1845. In 1836 an overseer listed the first names of 77 people who had worked seven days a week to bring in that year’s cotton; in April 1830 a Prud’homme cousin sold Phanor Prud’homme a couple, Thibuad and Salinette, and their six children for just over $3,000. The Historic Resource Study cautions that almost everything recorded about these lives was written by planters and overseers. [n]

The brochure describes the cotton year: picking began in August and ran from first light until too dark to see, the hard bolls cut pickers’ hands, and the overseer expected each adult to pick at least 200 pounds a day. [n]

CAHA.name: Cape Hatteras National Seashore
CAHA.summary: Cape Hatteras National Seashore, established in 1953, was the first national seashore in the United States. Stretching across portions of North Carolina's Outer Banks barrier islands — Bodie Island, Hatteras Island, and Ocracoke Island — the seashore protects over 30,000 acres of dynamic coastline shaped by wind, waves, and storms. The waters off Cape Hatteras, where the cold Labrador Current meets the warm Gulf Stream, have been known as the "Graveyard of the Atlantic" for the more than 1,000 shipwrecks documented in the area. The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, at 198.5 feet the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States, was famously relocated 2,900 feet inland in 1999 to save it from shoreline erosion.

CANY.name: Canyonlands National Park
CANY.summary: Canyonlands National Park in southeastern Utah preserves 337,598 acres of dramatic desert landscape carved by the Colorado and Green Rivers into countless canyons, mesas, and buttes. Established as a national park in 1964 through the efforts of Secretary of the Interior Stewart Udall, Canyonlands is divided into four distinct districts: Island in the Sky, The Needles, The Maze, and the rivers themselves. The region's geological record spans over 300 million years, and archaeological evidence shows human presence dating back at least 10,000 years, including ancestral Puebloan granaries and Fremont rock art.

CARI.summary:
A branch of the New World culture called Creole took root along the Cane River in 18th-century Louisiana, at what the Park Service calls the borderlands between New France and New Spain — a culture nurtured by French and Spanish colonial ways, steeped in Africanisms and enriched by American Indian contact. Cane River Creole National Historical Park preserves two of its plantations, Oakland and Magnolia, 10 and 20 miles south of Natchitoches: in the Park Service’s words the most intact French Creole cotton plantations in the United States, owned and worked by the same families, the Prud’hommes and the LeComte–Hertzogs, since the 18th century. Together they hold 70 historic structures, including eight rare brick slave quarters at Magnolia, and nearly 500,000 museum objects and archives. [n] [n]

Jean Baptiste Lecomte obtained the land grant that grew into Magnolia in 1753; Emmanuel Prud’homme received the grant at the core of Bermuda, later renamed Oakland, in 1789, and after the cotton gin’s invention in 1793 both families turned to cotton; enslaved workers built Prud’homme’s house in 1821. After the United States took possession of Louisiana in 1803, the park’s 2018 brochure explains, Anglo-American settlers poured in with their English language, Protestant religion and their own enslaved workers; life grew more constricted for non-whites as U.S. law removed colonial-era rights such as self-emancipation by purchase. [n]

Congress created the park on November 2, 1994, in the same law that created the 116,000-acre Cane River National Heritage Area — the only time a park unit and a heritage area have been legislated together. The Park Service says the park tells the story of oppressive plantation labor systems founded on slavery and replaced by tenant farming, sharecropping and day labor through the 1970s. [n]

black.html:
After the war a Union commander, on June 5, 1865, told freed people to stay on the premises to which they belonged, and Freedmen’s Bureau contracts at Bermuda paid six to ten dollars a month for men and five to eight for women. Those contracts, the park’s brochure says, differed from slavery mainly in requiring the worker’s consent; sharecropping ranged from a relatively benign feudalism to virtual bondage, the chains of slavery replaced by endless debt at the plantation store. Many stayed and rebuilt a community around church and family, often in the quarters that had housed their enslaved ancestors. [n] [n]

The first sharecropper did not leave Oakland until 1949. At Magnolia the Hertzogs housed day laborers in the brick cabins, which got electricity in the 1940s; mechanical pickers replaced the field crews in the 1960s, and the last residents, the Vercher family, moved out in the early 1970s. [n] [n]

indigenous.html:
Before there was a French post at Natchitoches, this valley was Caddo country. By the end of the 1400s the Caddo numbered about 200,000, and the Red River valley was among the most densely settled parts of their homeland. Then came European disease and a years-long drought: archaeological evidence cited in the 2019 Historic Resource Study suggests the population fell by about 95 percent between 1500 and the 1680s. The Natchitoches confederacy, smallest of three, lived in villages on the river terraces between today’s Oakland Plantation and Natchitoches. [n]

In 1835 the Caddo sold all their lands by a treaty signed near Shreveport, for $30,000 in goods and horses and a promise of $50,000 over five years, pledging never to return to live as a nation within the United States. They went to Texas and later to Oklahoma, where the Caddo Nation is based today. Some stayed or returned, and the tribe still holds the Natchitoches area as its spiritual homeland. [n]

sources.title: Historic Resource Study: Cane River Creole National Historical Park (Commonwealth Heritage Group & Suzanne Turner Associates for NPS, 2019)

slavery.html:
Slavery built both plantations. Between 1810 and 1860 the Prud’hommes held between 50 and 145 people, placing them in the top nine percent of Louisiana slaveholders. The LeComtes held 234 people in 1860 across Magnolia and their other properties, 112 of them in the Magnolia quarters, completed in 1845. In 1836 an overseer listed the first names of 77 people who had worked seven days a week to bring in that year’s cotton; in April 1830 a Prud’homme cousin sold Phanor Prud’homme a couple, Thibuad and Salinette, and their six children for just over $3,000. The Historic Resource Study cautions that almost everything recorded about these lives was written by planters and overseers. [n]

The brochure describes the cotton year: picking began in August and ran from first light until too dark to see, the hard bolls cut pickers’ hands, and the overseer expected each adult to pick at least 200 pounds a day. [n]

CASA.summary:
On the west bank of Matanzas Bay at St. Augustine stands the oldest masonry fort in the continental United States: a hollow square of locally quarried coquina stone, with a diamond-shaped bastion at each corner and only one way in. Spain broke ground on October 2, 1672, and finished it in 1695, replacing nine successive wooden forts that had guarded the town since its founding in 1565. For many years it was the northernmost outpost of Spain’s empire in the Americas, built to protect the town and the Gulf Stream route of the treasure fleets. [1] [1]

It held. English forces besieged it for 50 days in 1702, and British troops bombarded it for 27 days in 1740; the Park Service notes that the Castillo changed hands only by treaty, never in battle — to Britain in 1763, back to Spain in 1783, to the United States in 1821. The Americans renamed it Fort Marion and made it a prison for Native people: Seminoles in 1837, Plains Indians from 1875 to 1878, Apaches in 1886–1887. Proclaimed a national monument in 1924 and transferred to the Park Service in 1933, it had its Spanish name restored by Congress in 1942. [1] [1]

The Park Service defines the monument’s purpose as preserving the fort and interpreting more than 450 years of cultural intersections. Its seawall is now the lowest point in St. Augustine’s seawall network, which makes the fort the first place in the city to flood in a storm. [1] [1]

black.html: Africans were here from the start: Menéndez arrived in 1565 with about 50 Africans, free and enslaved, among his 800 colonists. When disease cut down the Native workforce building the Castillo, Governor Manuel de Cendoya asked Cuba for thirty enslaved Africans. In 1687 eleven people escaped slavery in Carolina by boat and reached St. Augustine; the governor refused to return them, and six of the men were paid to work on the Castillo. A 1693 royal decree offered freedom to those who fled British colonies and converted, and in 1738 Governor Manuel de Montiano granted the freedom seekers land two miles north of town. Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose — Fort Mose — was, the Park Service says, the first legally established free African settlement in North America, about a hundred people led by militia captain Francisco Menéndez. When Spain ceded Florida in 1763, its people left for Cuba. [1] [1]

sources.title: NPS, Castillo de San Marcos: African Americans in St. Augustine 1565–1821 (nps.gov)
Palmer, Forgotten Sacrifice, Florida Historical Quarterly 80(4), 2002, p. 447

climate.html:
The 2025 environmental assessment for the seawall that fronts the fort is blunt. The wall is aging, eroding and storm-damaged, its low elevation worsened by subsidence, and coquina is porous: running water wears it, and acidic rain and seawater can dissolve the shell in the stone. Under the intermediate sea-level scenario the designers chose — about one meter of global rise by 2100 — the North and South Wall segments would be overtopped by Matanzas Bay even without a storm, with the potential to flood historic St. Augustine. Both of the Park Service’s action alternatives would raise the North and South wall segments to an elevation of +10.5 feet. [1]

The 2016 foundation document had already listed rising seas, rising groundwater, possible saltwater intrusion and more intense storms among the threats to the Castillo itself. [1]

indigenous.html:
The fort was built with Native labor. Jason Palmer’s 2002 study documents Apalachee, Timucua and Guale men drafted under Spain’s labor system to quarry coquina on Anastasia Island and burn oyster shell for lime; the Apalachee quota rose from 100 to 300 men a year, and disease, hunger and exhaustion killed many. The walls, Palmer concludes, could not protect the people who built them. [1]

As Fort Marion it became an Army prison. In 1875, 74 prisoners chosen at Fort Sill — Cheyenne, Kiowa, Comanche, Arapaho and Caddo, many survivors of the 1864 Sand Creek Massacre — were brought here (the same Park Service page later gives the number as seventy-two). They were first kept in chains and shackles, which were removed after their jailer, Lt. Richard Henry Pratt, took charge; they were released in 1878. Their ledger drawings survive in the park collection. In 1886 came Chiricahua and Warm Springs Apaches, many of them women and children — more than 500 people, by Omega East and Albert Manucy’s 1952 account — crowded into some 130 tents atop the fort. The park now holds gatherings with the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes to honor those imprisoned here. [1] [1] [1]

latino.html:
St. Augustine, founded by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés in 1565, is the oldest permanent European settlement in the continental United States, and for 235 years it was the political, military and religious capital of Spanish Florida. Its grid of narrow streets, plaza and patios may be the earliest example of community planning in the continental United States, and the brochure says the city’s character still reflects its Spanish heritage. The Castillo was laid out by the Spanish engineer Ignacio Daza; it was a presidio, and no one lived inside — soldiers lived in town with their families and came to the fort for 24-hour guard shifts. Spain’s Florida missions predate those of the American West by more than a century. [1]

The Park Service calls the fort a symbol of America’s first great melting pot, where Native people, European soldiers and settlers, and enslaved and free Africans met and clashed. [1]

CAWO.name: Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site
CAWO.summary: The Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site in Washington, D.C., preserves the residence and workplace of Dr. Carter G. Woodson (1875–1950), the scholar known as the "Father of Black History." Woodson, the second African American to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard University (after W.E.B. Du Bois), founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History in 1915, established the Journal of Negro History in 1916, and created Negro History Week in 1926 — which later became Black History Month. He lived and worked in the Shaw neighborhood rowhouse from 1922 until his death in 1950. The site was designated a national historic site in 2006.

CHOH.name: C&O Canal NHP
CHOH.summary: The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park preserves the 184.5-mile towpath and canal route that runs from Georgetown in Washington, D.C. to Cumberland, Maryland, paralleling the Potomac River. Constructed between 1828 and 1850, the C&O Canal was conceived as a transportation route to connect the eastern seaboard with the Ohio River valley, but competition from the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad ultimately limited the canal's commercial success. The canal ceased operations in 1924 after a devastating flood, and a campaign led by Supreme Court Justice William O. Douglas in 1954 helped save the corridor from being converted into a highway. It was designated a national historical park in 1971.

CHPI.summary:
Snee Farm, 28 acres in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, is the last undeveloped piece of a 715-acre Lowcountry plantation that Colonel Charles Pinckney bought in 1754. His son Charles, born in Charleston on October 26, 1757, inherited it in 1782 and used it as a country retreat; George Washington stopped there for breakfast in May 1791. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 the younger Pinckney attended every session and submitted a draft constitution that was never formally considered. The park’s foundation document credits him with more than 25 clauses in the final Constitution; the park brochure says his draft contained 30 or more provisions that were incorporated into the final document. [1] [1]

No building from the Pinckney era still stands. Most of his papers burned in Charleston’s 1861 fire, and the plantation was sold to pay his debts in 1817; the cypress-and-pine cottage on the site today dates from about 1828. What is known of the Pinckney years has come largely out of the ground: archeologists have recovered more than 150,000 artifacts, including the slave-made earthenware called Colonoware, and have located the kitchen, the well and two slave cabins. [1] [1]

The rest of the land was sold for housing development and a golf course in the early 1970s, and in 1986 a developer began grading roads across the remaining core. Local residents organized the Friends of Historic Snee Farm, Congress established the historic site on September 8, 1988, and the Park Service acquired the 28 acres in 1990. Its foundation document charges it with interpreting the lives of the farm’s inhabitants, “enslaved as well as free” — a place that was, in the park’s own words, home and livelihood to some and “a form of prison” to others. [1] [1]

black.html:
By 1790 the Lowcountry parishes were nearly 70 percent Black, and the HRS describes how the relative isolation of large plantations let enslaved people blend African traditions into the culture and creole language now called Gullah. After emancipation, African Americans kept working Snee Farm as tenants, sharecroppers and wage laborers. A 2001 park study by Tyson Gibbs of the University of North Texas anthropology department, built on oral-history interviews with former Snee Farm workers and their relatives, recorded Black foremen who ran the farm for its owners between 1943 and 1968 — Charlie Stroder, Billie Seabrook and members of the Kinsey family — and workers who moved freely between Snee Farm and Boone Hall across the road. [1] [1]

Gibbs found that African Americans, more than 75 percent of the area’s people at the first census, had fallen to about 7 percent of Mount Pleasant’s population, and warned of shrinking neighborhoods, developers’ demand for Black-owned land and the scattering of a culture. [1]

slavery.html:
The park’s 2000 Historic Resource Study notes that a 1787 inventory listed forty enslaved people at Snee Farm, among them a gardener, carpenters, coopers and Cudjoe, a driver and sawyer; the 1810 census counted 58. They grew rice and indigo, and the study traces Lowcountry tidal-rice methods to West Africa and notes that planters relied heavily on enslaved people’s knowledge to produce the crop. The study finds archeological evidence that the “task” system prevailed at Snee Farm; shells, bones and a lead shot found in a cabin posthole hint at the food they caught for themselves. Their village of post-in-ground houses, one measuring 16 by 20 feet, stood about 250 yards from the planter’s house and was in use from about 1750 to 1841. [1] [1]

The same study notes that at the Convention Pinckney defended slavery against Northern delegates and fought for the three-fifths clause, for continuing the importation of enslaved Africans until 1808, and for the fugitive slave clause. When Snee Farm was sold in 1817, 43 people were enslaved there. [1]

CHRI.summary:
On the harbor of St. Croix’s northeast coast, a three-block stretch of waterfront holds what the Park Service calls one of the most complete and best-preserved groups of 18th- and 19th-century Danish colonial buildings in the New World: Fort Christiansvaern, the Danish West India & Guinea Company Warehouse, the Customs House, the Scale House where hogsheads of sugar and puncheons of rum were weighed for export, and the Steeple Building, St. Croix’s first Lutheran church. The Danish company bought the island from France in 1733 and laid out Christiansted, named for King Christian VI, around a good harbor; a remarkably progressive 1747 building code shaped its orderly growth, and its neoclassical buildings still offer arcaded sidewalks and breezy galleries. [1] [1] [1]

The wealth in those walls was made by enslaved Africans. In 1803 St. Croix had 30,000 people, 26,500 of them enslaved, working cane on 218 plantations, and for a time it was one of the wealthiest sugar islands in the West Indies. The Park Service names the site’s central significance plainly: this is where tens of thousands of enslaved Africans were landed and sold at auction. Slavery was abolished in 1848. The United States bought the islands for $25 million in gold, and the transfer at Fort Christiansvaern and two other venues on March 31, 1917, created the U.S. Virgin Islands. [1] [1]

Civic-minded residents petitioned the federal government to protect the fort and its buildings, and the site was established as Virgin Islands National Historic Site on March 4, 1952. [1]

black.html: In slavery’s shadow a distinct class of Free Blacks grew up on St. Croix. Some were freed for service; others bought their freedom with money earned as artisans or from produce sold at the Sunday Market. They worked as merchants, fishermen, seamen, tailors, coopers and blacksmiths, filled the fire brigade and served in the militia, and many of the anonymous masons and carpenters who built Christiansted’s neoclassical town were Free Blacks. As early as 1747 a section of town, Neger Gotted — later Free Gut — was set aside for them to build their own houses. Their number more than doubled between 1791 and 1815, from 775 to 1,764, but not until 1834 were they granted full equality with whites. [1]

sources.title: NPSHistory.com: Christiansted archive page — brochure text (2004): Free Blacks; In the West Indian Style; Regulars and Militia

indigenous.html: St. Croix’s first settlers came up the Lesser Antilles from South America. By 2,000 years ago there was a village at Salt River Bay on the north shore, and by 1300 it had the only ceremonial plaza and ball court so far found in the Lesser Antilles. On his second voyage, in 1493, Columbus named the island Santa Cruz and sent a boat ashore; it met Kalinago people (the brochure calls them Caribs) in a canoe, and the fight that followed, at what became known as the Cape of the Arrows, is considered the first armed resistance to European encroachment in the Americas. Over the next century the Spanish wiped out the island’s Kalinago population. The park’s museum holds what it calls a world-class archeological collection documenting St. Croix’s Amerindian cultures. [1] [1] [1]

slavery.html:
From settlement in 1734 until Denmark ended its slave trade — in 1803, by the park brochure’s dating — tens of thousands of Africans — the exact number is not known — were shipped to St. Croix. Survivors of the Middle Passage were auctioned at the Company’s compound — a warehouse complex built by enslaved Africans the Company owned, where, the Park Service says, people were sold in the courtyard until the 1750s. On the plantations they worked dawn to dark six days a week and around the clock at harvest, lived in masonry huts they built themselves in rows arranged for control, and kept African language, religion and foods alive. [1] [1]

Captured leaders of the 1733 uprising on St. John helped build the fort; in the early 1800s its prison held mostly enslaved plantation workers. Beside its doors, exposed ground marks the whipping post where enslaved people were publicly brutalized. The fort is now part of the National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom. [1] [1] [1]

COLO.summary:
Colonial National Historical Park holds both ends of British America on one Virginia peninsula: Jamestown Island on the James River, where 104 Englishmen came ashore in 1607, and the fields at Yorktown on the York, where Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781. The Colonial Parkway runs between them through bald cypress, marsh and pine-hardwood forest, and about 6,000 of the park’s 8,677 acres are habitat for native plants and wildlife. People lived here for more than 11,000 years before the English arrived; the park’s 2018 foundation document says its resources evoke the interaction and conflict between the colonists and the Powhatan Paramount Chiefdom, the evolution of the colonies, and the development of lifelong African American slavery. [1] [2]

In 1619 the first elected representative assembly in English-speaking North America — 22 burgesses, subject to the governor’s veto — met in the church at Jamestown. The same year, 20 to 30 captive Africans were sold at Point Comfort. The park’s brochure puts the two side by side and draws the conclusion itself: Jamestown’s legacy includes representative government, but also slavery, a brutal institution that spread through the colonies. Congress authorized the park in 1930; the Park Service bought most of Jamestown Island in 1934, and in 1994 Preservation Virginia’s Jamestown Rediscovery project began the search that found the original James Fort, long believed lost to the river. [1] [2]

climate.html: Jamestown Island is low, sinking and surrounded by water. Sea level here rose an average of 0.18 inch a year between 1927 and 2013 and could stand 2.1 to 2.7 feet higher by 2100, and land subsidence on the island amplifies the rise. Recent assessments of more than fifty archeological sites on the island recorded dramatic losses to coastal erosion, many of them 40 to 50 percent. The park’s average temperature rose at a rate of 1.2 °C per century from 1950 to 2010, and the 2018 foundation document expects erosion and inundation to further damage and destroy archeological resources, storm surge to threaten the Jamestown collections storage and the parkway’s riverside stretches along the James and York, and rising seas to worsen scour at some parkway bridge abutments. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Colonial National Historical Park, Virginia (NPS, May 2018)

indigenous.html: The English landed inside the chiefdom of Wahunsenacawh, known as Powhatan, who ruled subordinate tribes from Werowocomoco. The foundation document says he first tried to absorb the colony as one more tributary “tribe,” then to contain rather than destroy it; a key source of conflict was the colonists’ demand for food the tribes could not spare, after drought-induced crop failures that NPS-sponsored tree-ring analyses of Jamestown’s cypresses have since revealed. When more English arrived, Powhatan cut off the maize and besieged the fort, and the Starving Time of 1609–10 followed. His brother Opechancanough led attacks in 1622 and 1644, by which time disease and English attacks had set the confederacy’s power in decline. After Opechancanough was captured and killed in 1646, his successor’s treaty made the confederacy’s tribes tributaries of the English king and established one of the earliest Indian reservations; after Bacon’s Rebellion, the 1677 Treaty of Middle Plantation added tributary tribes and formalized a reservation for the Pamunkey and Mattaponi, a treaty the foundation document says is still in effect. The Pamunkey and the Catawba Indian Nation are the park’s traditionally associated tribes. [2] [1]

sources.title: Foundation Document, Colonial National Historical Park, Virginia (NPS, May 2018)
NPSHistory.com: Colonial National Historical Park archive page — overview (from the 2018 NPS brochure) and establishment block

slavery.html: Tobacco, which John Smith said passed in Virginia as current silver, demanded labor. At first the colony relied on indentured servants, and the earliest Africans faced conditions closer to theirs; some bought their freedom and became planters. The foundation document traces how that changed: the number of enslaved Africans in Virginia rose from 300 in 1650 to 13,000 in 1700; after 1662 a child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life; and after Bacon’s Rebellion, in which many Black indentured servants fought, new laws were meant to divide poor whites and Blacks. The 1705 Slave Code, in the brochure’s words, stripped all rights from people of color. At the New Town home site of planter-merchant William Pierce, archeologists are uncovering the story of a woman named Angelo or Angela, the only one of the first Africans whose name is known, who lived in his household in 1625. [2] [1]

CUGA.name: Cumberland Gap NHP
CUGA.summary: Cumberland Gap National Historical Park straddles the border of Kentucky, Virginia, and Tennessee at a natural pass through the Appalachian Mountains that has served as a major migration corridor for thousands of years. Herds of bison and Native American peoples — including Cherokee and Shawnee — used the gap long before European settlement. In 1775, Daniel Boone led a party to widen the trail through the gap into what became the Wilderness Road, and by 1810 an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 settlers had passed through Cumberland Gap heading west. The park was authorized by Congress in 1940 and encompasses over 24,000 acres of forested mountain terrain.

CUIS.name: Cumberland Island National Seashore
CUIS.summary: Cumberland Island National Seashore protects Georgia's largest and southernmost barrier island — an 18-mile-long island encompassing over 36,000 acres of maritime forest, salt marshes, tidal creeks, and undeveloped beaches. The island has a layered human history stretching from the Timucuan people through Spanish missions, British colonial settlement, and the plantation era. After the Civil War, formerly enslaved people established the First African Baptist Church on the island, which still stands today. In the late 19th century, industrialist Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy built several grand estates on the island. The national seashore was established in 1972 to protect the island's natural and cultural resources from development.

EVER.name: Everglades NP
EVER.summary: Everglades National Park, established in 1947, protects 1.5 million acres of tropical and subtropical wetlands at the southern tip of Florida — the largest subtropical wilderness in the United States. It was the first national park created to protect a biological ecosystem rather than scenic grandeur. The park's "River of Grass," as described by Marjory Stoneman Douglas in her influential 1947 book, is a slow-moving sheet of water that flows southward from Lake Okeechobee to Florida Bay. The Everglades provides habitat for 36 federally listed threatened or endangered species, including the Florida panther, American crocodile, and West Indian manatee. It is designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, an International Biosphere Reserve, and a Wetland of International Importance.

FIIS.name: Fire Island National Seashore
FIIS.summary: Fire Island National Seashore, established in 1964, protects a 26-mile stretch of barrier island off the southern shore of Long Island, New York — one of the last remaining undeveloped barrier beaches on the Atlantic Coast. The national seashore was created after a fierce conservation battle to prevent large-scale resort development on the island. The park includes the Sunken Forest, a rare 300-year-old maritime holly forest growing behind the dunes, and the Fire Island Lighthouse, first constructed in 1826 and rebuilt in 1858. The William Floyd Estate, the ancestral home of a signer of the Declaration of Independence, is also part of the seashore. Fire Island has historically served as a significant cultural refuge for LGBTQ communities, particularly the communities of Cherry Grove and Fire Island Pines.

FODA.name: Fort Davis National Historic Site
FODA.summary: Fort Davis National Historic Site in the Davis Mountains of West Texas preserves one of the best surviving examples of a frontier military post in the American Southwest. Established in 1854, the fort guarded emigrants, mail coaches, and freight wagons on the San Antonio–El Paso road through Limpia Canyon. After the Civil War, the post was garrisoned by troops of the 9th and 10th U.S. Cavalry and the 24th and 25th U.S. Infantry — the famed Buffalo Soldiers, African American troops who played a vital role in the frontier Army during the Indian Wars period. The fort was active until 1891 and was designated a national historic site in 1963. Over two dozen original and restored buildings remain, making it one of the most intact frontier forts in the West.

FODO.name: Fort Donelson National Battlefield
FODO.summary: Fort Donelson National Battlefield in Dover, Tennessee, preserves the site of the first major Union victory in the Civil War. In February 1862, forces under Brigadier General Ulysses S. Grant captured the Confederate river fortification on the Cumberland River after a combined land and naval assault. The surrender of roughly 12,000 Confederate troops — the largest surrender of American forces up to that point — opened the door for Union control of middle and western Tennessee and earned Grant the nickname "Unconditional Surrender" Grant. The battlefield was established as a national military park in 1928 and redesignated a national battlefield in 1985.

FOFR.summary:
On St. Simons Island, Georgia, at a sharp bend in the Frederica River between salt marsh and live oaks hung with moss, lie the remains of Frederica, the fort and town James Oglethorpe laid out in 1736 to hold Britain’s southern frontier against Spanish Florida. The first settlers — 44 men, mostly skilled workers, and 72 women and children — built palmetto huts and then houses of wood, brick and tabby, a concrete of burnt oyster shell, along a 75-foot-wide Broad Street shaded by orange trees. At its height the town held about 500 people by the 2009 park brochure’s count, more than 800 by the 2016 foundation document’s. [1] [2]

Frederica was born of war. In early 1740 “the aggressive Oglethorpe,” as the 2009 brochure calls him, set out to capture St. Augustine with 900 troops and 1,100 Indian allies, and failed. In July 1742 a Spanish force landed on the island; British troops beat back one column within sight of the town and ambushed another at Bloody Marsh. Casualties were light, but within a week the Spanish withdrew, ending, in the Park Service’s judgment, Spain’s claim to Georgia and the Carolinas. Peace undid the town: the regiment was disbanded in 1749, and a visitor in 1755 found houses without inhabitants and streets overgrown with weeds. [1] [2]

Congress created the national monument on May 26, 1936. Its roughly 282 acres in two units protect a largely intact archeological record — the subject of more than 40 investigations since 1936, with more than 227,000 objects in the park’s collections — and tabby ruins such as the King’s Magazine that now stand in the path of an eroding riverbank. [2]

black.html: Just outside the town wall lies a small cemetery of freed people from the late 1860s and 1870s. One of them is Thomas Abbott, whom Charles Stevens — a coastal shipper who held nineteen people in slavery in 1860 and whose family owned much of the old townsite — had enslaved; another is Celia Abbott. Many freed people, the park notes, still worked for former enslavers after emancipation, often on the same land. Thomas Abbott’s son Robert, born on St. Simons, founded The Chicago Defender, a paper that aided African Americans during the Great Migration and exposed lynching; in 1928 he paid $1,500 for a monument to his ancestors. Ground-penetrating radar in 2017 and 2019 and a 2019 excavation, guided by a church map marking a “Colored burial lot,” confirmed the cemetery’s location. The monument, the 2016 foundation document says, links the park to the island’s African American community and the early struggle against racial prejudice. [6] [2]

climate.html: The river beside which Oglethorpe placed Frederica is now eroding it. The 2016 foundation document warns that shoreline erosion along the Frederica River is an increasing threat, especially to the King’s Magazine, and that a rising water table and more frequent and intense storm surges tied to climate change could disturb buried archeological deposits. Salt marshes on the Georgia coast, it notes, may shrink by 20 to 40 percent this century as sea level rises. The document calls for working with Georgia’s Department of Natural Resources on a Living Shoreline project to stabilize the bank, and one of its interpretive themes concerns conserving and restoring the island ecology that shaped the lives of the people who lived there. [2]

indigenous.html: Before Frederica there was a Guale village on the same ground, allied to Spain through trade and conversion to Catholicism; two Spanish missions stood on the island. The park’s history describes how English traders armed Native slave raiders — the Westo were the largest such group from 1679 into the early 1700s — and how British colonists and their allies attacked the coastal missions to enslave the Guale; in 1683 the village and missions were abandoned, their people following the Spanish south or forcibly removed. Half a century later the Yamacraw, a people of mixed Creek and Yamasee descent, served as treaty negotiators between Oglethorpe and the Creek, allowing Frederica’s peaceful founding in February 1736. Oglethorpe laid out the town lots on a field the Indians had planted in corn, and townspeople traded with Creek and Yuchi people outside the town gate. [3] [1]

slavery.html: Frederica’s settlers farmed with their own hands, because Georgia banned slavery. The park attributes the ban both to the Trustees’ ideals and to fear: an enslaved person’s quickest way to freedom ran down the Frederica River to Spanish Florida, where accepting Catholicism and fighting for Spain could bring liberty. Colonists petitioned against the ban soon after Frederica’s founding; in 1751 Parliament allowed slavery. By 1775 nearly 18,000 people were enslaved in Georgia; St. Simons came to hold more than 14 plantations. In 1803 John Couper and Thomas Spalding bought 75 Igbo people in Savannah; on the voyage south, the park recounts, they overpowered their captors, took the ship into Dunbar Creek two miles from Frederica, and walked into the water rather than be re-enslaved. Long told as legend — the park notes details vary by source — the event is documented in letters to Pierce Butler, one recording bodies salvaged at ten dollars a head. [1] [5]

women.html: Coosaponakeesa, known as Mary Musgrove, was born at Coweta on the Ocmulgee River in 1700, the daughter of British trader Edmund Griffen and of a sister of the Lower Creek leader Brim. When Oglethorpe met the Yamacraw chief Tomochichi in 1733 she interpreted, and the colony paid her one hundred pounds sterling a year. She helped negotiate treaties, recruited warriors against Spain, supplied the struggling colonists with meat and bread, and in 1742 influenced the Creeks to aid the British on St. Simons. She owned three trading posts, and her third husband, Thomas Bosomworth, pressed claims to Sapelo, St. Catherine’s and Ossabaw islands granted to her by the Creeks — making her, in the park’s telling, the largest landowner in colonial Georgia. [4]

FOMC.name: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine
FOMC.summary: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine in Baltimore, Maryland, is the birthplace of the American national anthem. During the Battle of Baltimore on September 13–14, 1814, British naval forces bombarded the star-shaped fort for 25 hours during the War of 1812. The fort's successful defense inspired Francis Scott Key, who watched the bombardment from a truce ship in the harbor, to write the poem "Defence of Fort M'Henry," which was later set to music and became "The Star-Spangled Banner," officially adopted as the national anthem in 1931. Designated as a national park in 1925 and redesignated in 1939, Fort McHenry is the only unit in the National Park System designated both a national monument and a historic shrine.

FORA.summary:
At the wooded north end of Roanoke Island, behind the Outer Banks, English explorers attempted to create England’s first colonial settlement in the New World. In 1585 a military party of 108 colonists built a small earthen fort here and left within a year; in 1587 a second colony of about 110 men, women and children arrived, and when John White returned in 1590 he found only the letters “CRO” carved on a tree and “CROATOAN” carved on a palisade post. Of some 250 colonists who struggled here, 116 men, women and children disappeared. The 355-acre site preserves the reconstructed fort — the only structure whose location is known exactly — and the ground where part, perhaps all, of the settlement stood. [1] [2]

The island holds more than the mystery. The Park Service calls it the site of the first sustained interaction between Native Americans and the English, which produced the first written cultural and ethnographic information of the Algonquian peoples of coastal North Carolina. Created by secretarial order on April 5, 1941, the park had its purpose broadened by Congress in 1990 to include the Native Americans, European Americans and African Americans who lived on the island — among them the 3,500 formerly enslaved people who built the Roanoke Island Freedmen’s Colony during and after the Civil War. [2] [3]

black.html: When Union forces took Roanoke Island in 1862, enslaved people from the island and the surrounding country fled to it — the first group, fifteen or twenty men, women and children, came down the Chowan River. They worked as porters, cooks and laundresses and built forts and docks; men were paid $10 a month and women and children $4. In 1863 Gen. John G. Foster ordered chaplain Horace James to found a colony on the island’s north end, where each family received a one-acre lot. By January 1865 there were at least 591 houses and more than 3,000 residents, with a church, several schools, a steam-powered saw and grist mill, and an appointed council of fifteen. It never became self-sufficient — many of its able-bodied young men enlisted in the Union Army — and James calculated the government owed the freedpeople more than $18,500 in unpaid wages. After the war the island’s prewar residents returned and reclaimed their land, rations were cut, and by February 1867 the colony had virtually dispersed. [3] [2]

climate.html: The island’s history now sits at the water’s edge. The 2017 foundation document reports archeological resources and their context being lost to shoreline erosion, warns that sea level rise may raise the water table and bring saltwater inundation and more severe storms to the earthen fort, and notes that the Waterside Theatre, home of The Lost Colony since 1937, stands directly against an eroding shoreline, where more storm surge, flooding and saltwater intrusion could hasten its decay. [2]

indigenous.html: The English came ashore among the Carolina Algonquians. In 1584 two of them, Manteo of the Croatoan and Wanchese of the Roanoke, sailed to England with the first expedition, and Thomas Hariot learned some of their language from them. The 1585 colonists, who planted little, came to depend on Indian food, robbed fish traps, and spread measles and smallpox; in 1586, at a parley he had arranged, Ralph Lane’s men opened fire on a prearranged signal and killed and beheaded the Roanoke leader Wingina. In 1587 White’s colonists attacked a village they wrongly believed hostile. Hariot himself rebuked colonists for killing Indians over offenses that might easily have been forgiven. The park’s foundation document concludes that the Carolina Algonquian, a culture nearly 1,000 years old, fell victim to the European race to capitalize on the New World until the culture and its people were extirpated, surviving only in archeological evidence and in the narratives, ethnography and art of the Roanoke voyages. [1] [3] [2]

labor_ccc.html: The New Deal remade the site before the Park Service owned it. From 1934, relief workers of the Works Progress Administration, under a state commission’s plan with structures designed by Frank Stick, built a juniper-log palisade, blockhouses, a chapel, a museum and other log buildings, several with thatch roofs, as a “highly conjectural” restoration of the 1587 settlement, and in 1937 WPA workers built the Waterside Theatre where Paul Green’s The Lost Colony opened. Visitation rose tenfold, to 30,000 in 1935. But Park Service historian Charles W. Porter found the blockhouse an 18th-century type that would suit the Pennsylvania frontier in 1776 and was absurd as “Fort Raleigh”; the administrative history concludes the log structures were historically inaccurate and had damaged archeologically sensitive ground. [4]

women.html: Raleigh’s second colony was meant to last, and so it carried families: seventeen women and nine children among the 110 colonists, seven of the women probably servants traveling alone. One was Eleanor Dare, John White’s daughter, who on August 18, 1587, gave birth to Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the New World. Nearly three centuries later, women ran the classrooms of the Freedmen’s Colony. Elizabeth James of the American Missionary Association began teaching from a log cabin in October 1863; by fall 1864 the school had seven teachers and still could not keep up with 1,297 children under fourteen and the many adults who wanted to learn to read and write. [3] [2]

FOSU.name: Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie NHP
FOSU.summary: Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, preserves the sites of the opening and closing engagements of the Civil War. On April 12, 1861, Confederate forces fired on the Union-held Fort Sumter, beginning the four-year conflict that would cost over 600,000 American lives. Fort Moultrie, on nearby Sullivan's Island, has an even longer military history — Patriot forces there repelled a British naval attack in 1776 during the Revolutionary War in one of the first decisive American victories. The park also interprets the role of Charleston Harbor as the main port of entry for enslaved Africans brought to North America, with an estimated 40 percent of all enslaved people entering the country passing through these waters.

FRRI.name: Freedom Riders National Monument
FRRI.summary: Freedom Riders National Monument in Anniston, Alabama, was designated by President Barack Obama in 2017 to preserve two sites associated with the 1961 Freedom Rides — the former Greyhound Bus Station in Anniston and the site outside the city where a mob firebombed a Greyhound bus carrying Freedom Riders on May 14, 1961. The Freedom Riders were interracial groups of civil rights activists who rode interstate buses into the segregated South to challenge the non-enforcement of Supreme Court rulings that declared segregated public buses unconstitutional. The brutal attacks in Anniston and Birmingham generated national and international outrage and ultimately led the Interstate Commerce Commission to enforce desegregation of interstate travel facilities.

FRST.summary:
Delaware is small, but the Park Service describes it as a state born out of a three-way contest among Sweden, the Netherlands and Great Britain for the Delaware Valley. First State National Historical Park gathers that story in seven places across Delaware’s two northern counties and a corner of Chester County, Pennsylvania: the rocks on the Christina River where Swedish and Finnish settlers landed in 1638; Holy Trinity (Old Swedes) Church, founded by their descendants in 1698; the New Castle Court House and its Green; the Green at Dover; John Dickinson’s plantation; and the 1,359-acre Brandywine Valley tract of farmsteads, wooded hillsides and stream valleys north of Wilmington. Long before any of them, the land was Lenape country. [1] [2]

On December 7, 1787, delegates meeting at the Golden Fleece Tavern on Dover’s Green made Delaware the first state to ratify the Constitution. President Barack Obama proclaimed the First State National Monument on March 25, 2013, and Congress made it a national historical park on December 19, 2014. The park’s own brochure frames its subject as more than 300 years in which people pursued human rights and self-determination on what it calls a fraught and uneven course, marked by questions and contradictions: the plantation of the primary author of the Articles of Confederation had free and enslaved laborers, and the courthouse where Delaware broke with Britain later saw two Quaker abolitionists bankrupted under the Fugitive Slave Act. The Rodneys, like the Ridgelys and the Dickinsons, owned large plantations near Dover; Caesar Rodney was among the leaders of the colony’s independence movement. [1] [2] [3]

black.html:
Delaware’s northern border was the line between slavery and freedom. In December 1845 Samuel D. Burris, a free Black man, guided Samuel and Emeline Hawkins and their six children from Maryland to Quaker John Hunn’s farm; Delaware’s chief justice found no evidence to hold the family, and Thomas Garrett sent them on to Pennsylvania. Convicted in a later case, Burris was sentenced to be sold into slavery for seven years until abolitionists posing as buyers rescued him at auction. In May 1848, in the New Castle Court House, Chief Justice Roger Taney and a jury of Sussex County men described in the study as predominantly pro-slavery found Hunn and Garrett liable under the 1793 Fugitive Slave Act; Taney’s $500 fine per fugitive bankrupted both men. [3] [2]

In the twentieth century, William Poole Bancroft’s Woodlawn Trustees excluded African Americans from their Woodlawn Flats housing in Wilmington, which as late as 1972 allowed only white residents. Only that year, after a decade of Quaker protest and a State Human Relations Commission investigation, did the Trustees agree to accept new applications “without regard to race, color or creed.” [3]

indigenous.html:
The Lenape knew the Delaware River as the Lenapewihittuck; “Delaware” was an English label — explorers named the bay for Virginia’s governor Lord De La Warr and applied the name to the Lenape themselves. Anthony F. C. Wallace estimated about 8,000 Lenape lived along its drainages around 1600. On the Big Bend of the Brandywine stood Queonemysing, “place where there are long fish,” a summer fishing village. In 1683 Seketarius — a principal Brandywine sachem who, Weslager believed, may have lived there — and other Lenape sachems promised to “give or sell” William Penn the land between the Christina and Upland creeks; in 1701 a Quaker settler was granted the village’s 200 acres on the claim that the people had left — to the surprise, the 2019 study notes, of a band that would have returned the next summer. [3]

Pushed west, the Lenape signed the first treaty the United States made with an Indian nation, at Fort Pitt in 1778. Under two 1829 treaties the federal government removed them to a reservation in Kansas; in 1867 most were moved again to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma), where they live today as the Delaware Tribe of Indians. [3] [2]

slavery.html: Kent County’s rich soil supported a plantation economy built on enslaved labor, and the John Dickinson Plantation is where the Park Service tells it. The Dickinsons grew wheat and grain there and held a large number of African Americans in bondage. On May 12, 1777, Dickinson signed a deed naming the men, women and children he held — Augustus, Joe, Toby, Mary, Flora, Dinah and many others — and promising them freedom only after another twenty-one years of faithful service. He reconsidered, freeing a few in 1781 and the rest in 1786; by the historic resource study’s count, fifty-nine people in all. Several stayed on as tenant farmers. Slavery remained legal in Delaware throughout the Civil War: nearly 9,000 people, about 15 percent of the state, were enslaved in 1790, and in 1860 there were still more than 1,300 in Sussex County, 303 in Kent and 254 in New Castle. [1] [3]

women.html: In 1920 the Nineteenth Amendment needed one more state, and suffragists hoped it would be the First State. Mabel Lloyd Ridgely, who lived on the Dover Green, had already, with the Colonial Dames, saved the old State House from a demolition the legislature proposed in 1909; she presided over the Delaware Equal Suffrage Association. Seven of the women arrested protesting in front of the White House in 1917 were Delawareans, among them Mabel Vernon and Florence Bayard Hilles. As rival rallies filled the Green, the state Senate ratified on May 5, 1920, but the House tabled the vote after nearly a month of debate — the brochure notes that declining to vote counted as a “no.” Anti-suffragists led by Delawareans Mary Wilson Thompson and Emily Bissell had come to Dover too. Hilles went on to work for passage in Tennessee, which ratified two months later; the amendment became law on August 26. [3] [2]

GATE.summary:
Gateway National Recreation Area wraps around the mouth of New York Harbor, an area known for more than a century as the “Gateway to America.” Its more than 26,000 acres reach from Sandy Hook in New Jersey along the south shore of Staten Island to Jamaica Bay and Breezy Point in New York — about 75 miles of shoreline, 31 of them ocean beach. Assembled from city parks, military posts and undeveloped land, it protects dunes, salt marsh islands and, at Sandy Hook, two globally imperiled kinds of barrier-island forest, maritime red-cedar woodland and maritime holly forest. More than 330 species of birds have been recorded here along the Atlantic Flyway. [1] [2]

The human story is as layered as the shoreline. The Sandy Hook Light, first lit in 1764, is the oldest continuously operating lighthouse in the nation; the Army opened its first weapons proving ground on the Hook in 1874; Fort Wadsworth guarded the Narrows for two centuries; and Floyd Bennett Field opened in 1931 as New York City’s first municipal airport, and during World War II the busiest military airport in the United States. [1] [2]

Congress established Gateway on October 27, 1972, as one of the first urban parks in the National Park System. Its foundation document counts more than 800 historic buildings, structures, landscapes and archeological sites, many already in poor condition when the park inherited them, and names the work ahead plainly: responding to climate change and sea level rise in a park most of whose natural and cultural resources lie beside the ocean and other water bodies. [1] [2]

black.html: Riis Park’s beach was rebuilt by Robert Moses under a 1936 plan, and in 1974 more than three million people visited its mile and a half of sand. When City University sociologists Terry Williams and William Kornblum studied it for the Park Service (the 2000 assessment dates their report to 1975), they found it organized into territories: on summer weekends Bay 5 was the beach of Black and Latin visitors — West Indians, Cubans, Puerto Ricans — with drums, card games and parties into the night; on one July 4th, they numbered perhaps 30,000 across the park. The authors observed pointedly that the crowd hardly matched the middle-class white family the Park Service was comfortable serving, and urged caution before strict enforcement. A 2000 ethnographic assessment for the Park Service found Bays 5 and 6 no longer solely a Black American area but popular with a diverse group of Black Caribbean Americans, Black Americans and Hispanics, a change it tied to twenty-five years of new immigration to Brooklyn and Queens from all over the world. [4] [5]
