climate.html: Most of Gateway’s natural and cultural resources sit beside the ocean and other water bodies, and its 2017 foundation document names responding to climate change and sea level rise as the first of the park’s key issues: the park has been changed by the frequency and intensity of recent storms such as Hurricane Sandy, some sites have already seen more flooding, and the park’s marshes and beaches serve as buffers that protect the neighborhoods behind them. When the document was written the park’s planning was still focused on recovering from Sandy. [2] A park climate poster on Jamaica Bay warns that its salt marsh islands, and the wildlife they shelter, are endangered by sea-level rise and human activity, showing Elders Point in 1951, when its restoration project started in 2006, and as restoration continued in 2010. [7]

indigenous.html: For thousands of years before the Dutch arrived, the northern shores of Jamaica Bay were home to the Canarsie, and the Rockaway peninsula to the Rechquaakie, “people of the sandy places” — both of the Lenape branch of the Algonquian peoples, according to the Park Service’s 2012 ethnographic overview. They gathered from the bay’s shellfish beds, leaving shoreline middens of oyster shell that the first European writers noticed, and, by early accounts, farmed a great cornfield that stretched for several miles across southeastern Brooklyn. From 1635, when Dutch settlers began building villages on land “purchased” from the Canarsie, warfare, disease and migration steadily weakened the Native communities; the authors date the death of the last known Canarsie person to 1830. Their legacy survives largely in place names: Rockaway, and perhaps Jamaica itself, which the report suggests may come from an old Algonquin word for “place of the beaver.” [3]

sources.title: Kornblum & Van Hooreweghe, The Changing Traditional Uses of Jamaica Bay, New York: Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS Northeast Region Ethnography Program, 2012), ch. 2

labor_ccc.html: The land under Floyd Bennett Field was once Barren Island, for much of the nineteenth century New York City’s offal depot and grease factory. A rendering and fish-oil industry began there in 1845; by 1884 about 500 people worked in its plants, and at its peak in the 1920s and early 1930s the island held close to 1,500 residents — African American, Irish, Italian and Polish families whose children picked over mountains of garbage while their parents worked the try works. The overview dates the eviction of the community to 1936, when Parks Commissioner Robert Moses had it razed for bridge approaches; one former resident, quoted in the overview, remembered only the western half being evicted and about 30 families staying on until 1939. Jane Shaw, for nineteen years the island school’s principal and only teacher, fought for time to let her pupils finish the school year and, in historian Benjamin Miller’s account, succeeded. The 2012 ethnographic overview suggests the eviction stands with the removal of Seneca Village for Central Park, as another example of the powerless being removed to create valuable public places. [3]

sources.title: Kornblum & Van Hooreweghe, The Changing Traditional Uses of Jamaica Bay (NPS, 2012), ch. 2, “The Legacy of Community Solidarity and Defended Neighborhoods”

lgbtq.html: At the eastern end of the beach, Bays 1 and 2 were, in the 1975 study, the home of a large gay community whose use of the beach, Williams and Kornblum reported, already went back more than twenty years; on an average day Bay 1 was about 70 percent gay and Bay 2 about 90 percent. They quoted Arthur Evans, writing in the gay publication The Advocate, on Riis as a haven — one place gay people could be openly themselves. A quarter-century later, the 2000 ethnographic assessment found that Bay 1 had retained its identity as a gay beach. Visitors described it as a space of freedom and liberation, one of the few beaches where they felt safe; some suspected that its neglected bathrooms and missing lifeguard reflected discrimination against them because, as they put it, they were gay and predominantly Black and Latino. In 2025 the Park Service listed Bay 1 as closed to swimming and access because of hazardous erosion. [4] [5] [6]

GLAC.summary:
Glacier National Park protects 1,600 square miles of the northern Rocky Mountains in Montana, where the plains end abruptly against peaks built of sediments laid down 1.5 billion years ago and shoved, about 75 million years ago, over far younger rock along the Lewis Overthrust. From Triple Divide Peak, water runs to the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico and Hudson Bay. Together with Waterton Lakes it is one of the few places in North America where all the native carnivores survive, and George Bird Grinnell named it the Crown of the Continent in 1908. [1] [2]

People have been drawn to this country for 10,000 years, and the park brochure calls it a landscape that has always been sacred to the Blackfeet, Salish and Kootenai peoples. Congress made Glacier the tenth national park on May 11, 1910; in 1932 it and Canada’s Waterton Lakes became the world’s first international peace park, later a biosphere reserve (1976) and World Heritage Site (1995). The park draws more than two million visitors a year; its Going-to-the-Sun Road, which crosses the Continental Divide at Logan Pass, was the first road designated a national historic civil engineering landmark. [2] [1]

The park’s namesakes are leaving. An estimated 150 glaciers existed around 1850; by 2015 only 26 remained large enough to count as active, and the 2016 foundation document describes the last remnants of alpine glaciers as disappearing quickly due to climate change. [4] [2]

climate.html: Glacier’s current ice is geologically young — formed about 7,000 years ago and at its largest around 1850, at the end of the Little Ice Age. Since 1900, the U.S. Geological Survey reports, the park region’s mean annual temperature has risen 1.33 °C, 1.8 times the global mean increase, and rain rather than snow has been the dominant form of the century’s added precipitation. Of the roughly 150 glaciers estimated in 1850, 26 were still active in 2015; Grinnell Glacier lost about 45 percent of its area between 1966 and 2015, and models project that some studied glaciers will disappear between 2030 and 2080. The loss reaches beyond scenery: glaciers act as a bank of water that keeps streams cold and flowing in late summer, and without meltwater, USGS warns, rising stream temperatures could cause local extinctions of sensitive aquatic species and harm the threatened bull trout. [4] [2]

sources.title: USGS, Retreat of Glaciers in Glacier National Park: 1996–2015 (2017), text and Glacier Area Summary table

indigenous.html:
The K’tunaxa (Kootenai) and the Piikáni, one of the three Blackfeet tribes, have ties to this country reaching back well over a thousand years; the mountains are the Piikáni’s most sacred place. On January 23, 1870, in what the 2001 ethnographic overview calls the Massacre on the Marias, Col. E. M. Baker, under orders from General Sheridan, attacked a winter camp of friendly Piikáni and killed 173 or more, mostly women, children and elders. In 1883–1885, as promised rations were delayed or never delivered, 400 to 600 Piikáni died. [3]

In September 1895 three commissioners, George Bird Grinnell among them, met Blackfeet leaders to buy the mountain lands. The Piikáni asked $3 million and received $1.5 million over ten years, plus the right to hunt, fish and cut timber while the land stayed public. The strip became part of Glacier National Park in 1910, and the government came to treat those rights as lost or severely curtailed; many Blackfeet contend they never gave them up. [3]

GLCA.name: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
GLCA.summary: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area in southern Utah and northern Arizona encompasses over 1.25 million acres of desert canyon country surrounding Lake Powell, the reservoir created by Glen Canyon Dam on the Colorado River. The dam, completed in 1966, was one of the most controversial reclamation projects in American history — its construction flooded hundreds of miles of canyon and thousands of archaeological sites, galvanizing the modern environmental movement. Author and conservationist Edward Abbey's writings about the area, particularly "Desert Solitaire" (1968), helped bring national attention to the ecological costs of damming western rivers. The recreation area also protects Rainbow Bridge National Monument, one of the world's largest natural bridges, sacred to the Navajo, Paiute, and other Indigenous nations.

GOGA.summary:
Golden Gate National Recreation Area wraps the mouth of San Francisco Bay: more than 80,000 acres across Marin, San Francisco and San Mateo counties, where the San Andreas Fault, the bay and the Pacific coastline converge. It reaches from the coast redwoods of Muir Woods, some nearly 1,000 years old, to the shoreline of Crissy Field and the former penitentiary on Alcatraz Island, and protects parts of 19 ecosystems and more than 1,250 plant and animal species, among them one of the largest concentrations of rare, threatened and endangered species in the national park system. These lands are the traditional homelands of the Coast Miwok and Ohlone peoples. [1]

The park’s forts and batteries run from Spanish settlement in 1776 to the Cold War Nike missile site in the Marin Headlands; the Presidio was a military post for more than 200 years, under Spain, briefly Mexico, and the United States from 1846. Alcatraz became the nation’s first military prison, then its most notorious federal penitentiary, then the site of the occupation that helped ignite the movement for American Indian self-determination. In 1972 Congress made it one of two experiments in bringing national parks to city dwellers, after Rep. Phillip Burton warned that without action the place where sea, bay and land meet would be doomed; it was established on October 27, 1972, and now draws more than 17 million visits a year. [2] [1]

black.html: Black soldiers garrisoned the Presidio at the turn of the twentieth century. In 1899 four companies of the 24th Infantry — veterans of Cuba, where they had nursed the sick in the Army hospital and lost many men to disease — arrived in San Francisco, three of them at the Presidio and one on Alcatraz; the 25th Infantry passed through on its way to the Philippines, and the 9th Cavalry was posted at the Presidio in 1900. When President Theodore Roosevelt visited in 1903, two troops of the 9th escorted him, the first time in the West, Daniels’s 1980 study notes, that Black soldiers held the place of honor in a public procession. In 1908 Black troops deserted at under one percent, against nearly five percent among white soldiers. Charles D. Young, a West Point graduate and in 1899 the Army’s only Black commissioned officer apart from chaplains, spoke across the Bay Area. [4] [1]

sources.title: Daniels, Afro-Americans, the San Francisco Bay Area, and the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, 1850–1960 (report for GGNRA, March 13, 1980), pp. 18–21

climate.html: The park’s 2025 coastal hazards assessment looked at 681 buildings and 433 roads, trails, piers and other transportation assets against flooding, shoreline change, sea-level rise and tsunami zones. Most sit high enough to escape, but 18 percent are highly or moderately vulnerable, clustered at Stinson Beach, Crissy Field, lower Fort Baker, Fort Cronkhite, Fort Mason and Point Bonita; the Fort Mason piers and the Alcatraz waterfront fall within every hazard zone evaluated. Coastal cliff retreat is a major concern in its own right: it has already brought down the Battery Bluff Panama Mounts at Fort Funston and threatens corridors such as Conzelman Road in the Marin Headlands. [5]

sources.title: Peek, Thompson, Tormey & Young, Coastal Hazards & Sea-Level Rise Asset Vulnerability Assessment for Golden Gate NRA, Presidio of San Francisco, and Fort Point NHS: Summary of Results (NPS 641/197620, May 2025), pp. 1–3

indigenous.html:
Before Spain arrived, the San Francisco Peninsula belonged to Ohlone people — called Costanoan, from the Spanish for “coast people,” in Kathryn Lang’s 1979 park study — living in small autonomous tribelets of about 200; the Ramaytush of San Francisco and San Mateo counties numbered about 1,400 in 1770. North of the strait, Coast Miwok territory, centered in Marin and Sonoma counties, took in much of today’s park. The Spanish garrison at the Presidio depended on their labor: mission Indians, some lent out and some sent as prisoners for alleged misconduct, built and constantly repaired its crumbling adobe walls and fortifications, with wages paid to the padres rather than the workers. Introduced disease ravaged the missions: Mission Dolores held 1,010 Indians in 1804 and only 241 less than twenty-five years later. [3]

Generations later, Indigenous people returned to claim a piece of the bay: the park’s foundation document credits the occupation of Alcatraz Island with helping to ignite the movement for American Indian self-determination. [1]

sources.title: Lang, Golden Gate National Recreation Area: The Indian and Hispanic Heritage of a Modern Urban Park (NPS, 1979), pp. 5, 8, 30, 107, 123

latino.html: Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portolá first saw San Francisco Bay in 1769 from Sweeney Ridge, now park land. On June 17, 1776, Lieutenant José Moraga led soldiers and settlers north from Monterey to build the fort at the site Juan Bautista de Anza had chosen — ten leather-jacket soldiers with their families, seven settler families, vaqueros and muleteers. The soldiers were mostly Mexican-born, and Lang’s 1979 study describes most of the colonists as poor families recruited in Sinaloa and Sonora. On September 17, 1776, they formally founded the Presidio of San Francisco with a Mass and the Spanish ceremony of possession. It served Spain, then briefly Mexico, until the United States took it in 1846, and the park’s foundation document dates its long line of fortifications from that Spanish settlement. [2] [3] [1]

GRCA.summary:
Grand Canyon is a twisting, 277-mile gorge of the Colorado River with thousands of miles of side canyons, carved over six million years. Its walls rise more than a mile above the river and expose one of the most complete geological records on Earth, from flat-lying layers that hold marine fossils down to basement rock as much as 1.84 billion years old. The park’s 1,218,375 acres run from Sonoran Desert at the bottom to conifer forest on the 8,000-foot North Rim, and 94 percent of it is managed as wilderness. [1] [1]

People have lived with the canyon for at least 12,000 years, and eleven federally recognized tribes keep strong historical, cultural and spiritual ties to it; the Navajo, Havasupai and Hualapai reservations share its boundary. President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed 818,560 acres a national monument on January 11, 1908; Congress made it a national park in 1919, and the 1975 Grand Canyon National Park Enlargement Act nearly doubled it, to more than 1.2 million acres. It became a World Heritage Site in 1979, and visitation, averaging about 4.5 million a year, reached 6 million in 2016. [1] [1]

The park’s own brochure points to the pressure on the river: Glen Canyon Dam now releases clearer, colder water in which native fish adapted to warmer, sediment-laden water cannot thrive, and the brochure asks whether one river can meet the Southwest’s growing demand. [1]

climate.html:
Grand Canyon is getting hotter. A 2024 Park Service report finds the park warmed significantly from 1895 to 2020 — 1.89 °F per century on average, and at a rate of 6.31 °F per century since 1970 — while total precipitation did not change significantly. Changes in the region already attributed at least in part to human-caused climate change include drier soils, reduced Colorado River flow and a doubling of the area burned by wildfire across the western United States; drawing on the literature, the report projects more drought, more large fires and worsening threats to archeological sites, cultural landscapes and historic structures. [1]

Mining is the other pressure. In 2012 Interior Secretary Ken Salazar closed federal lands in the Grand Canyon watershed to new mining claims until 2032, partly because, Interior found, impacts to tribal resources likely could not be mitigated. A USGS report published in 2024, co-written by Carletta Tilousi of the Havasupai Tribe, expands the risk framework for uranium mining to include the Havasupai perspective and applies it near Red Butte, a place sacred to the Havasupai, Hopi, Navajo and Zuni. [1]

sources.title: Lawrence et al., Historical and Projected Climate Change for Grand Canyon National Park and Surrounding Areas (NPS NRR 2024/2615), Executive Summary

indigenous.html:
A broken spear point found in Marble Canyon shows a hunter passing through about 11,000 years ago; Puebloan people were farming the rims and river deltas by about 1,500 years ago, and split-twig figurines, masonry rooms and rock art show that the canyon sheltered people for millennia — a span the brochure puts at 600 generations. Eleven tribes — Yavapai-Apache, Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, Kaibab Paiute, Las Vegas Paiute, Moapa Paiute, Navajo, Paiute Indian, San Juan Southern Paiute and Zuni — still use it for trade, gathering and ceremony. [1]

The park itself displaced people. Havasupai families farmed Ha’a Gyoh, below the South Rim, until Park Service policies forced them out in the 1920s; in 2022, at the tribe’s request, the place long called Indian Garden was renamed Havasupai Gardens, and the superintendent called the renaming long overdue. The 1975 enlargement act returned 83,800 acres of park land to the Havasupai Tribe and guaranteed traditional use of another 95,300. [1] [1]

women.html: Four buildings on the edge of the South Rim are the work of Mary Elizabeth Jane Colter, a Pittsburgh-born designer hired by the Fred Harvey Company and the Santa Fe Railway. Her Hopi House (1905) replicated part of the Hopi pueblo at Oraibi; Hermit’s Rest and Lookout Studio (both 1914) took their forms from the landscape, the studio rising out of the rim’s edge — “You can’t imagine what it cost to make it look this old,” she told railroad men who found Hermit’s Rest dingy. For the Desert View Watchtower, completed in 1932, she spent about six months studying ancestral Puebloan tower sites across the Southwest (Anasazi, in the form’s 1986 wording), and its Hopi Room murals are by the Hopi artist Fred Kabotie. A 1986 Park Service nomination argues that her landscape-shaped buildings helped form the architectural aesthetic for development in the national parks. [1]

GRSM.name: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
GRSM.summary: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, straddling the border of Tennessee and North Carolina, is the most visited national park in the United States, drawing over 12 million recreational visits annually. Established in 1934, the park protects 522,427 acres of old-growth temperate forest — one of the largest blocks of hardwood forest remaining in North America. The park's biodiversity is extraordinary: it is home to over 19,000 documented species and is often called the "Salamander Capital of the World" for its 30-plus salamander species. The Cherokee people inhabited the region for thousands of years before forced removal along the Trail of Tears in 1838; members of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians still reside on the adjacent Qualla Boundary. The park was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 and an International Biosphere Reserve in 1976.

GRTE.summary:
With no foothills in the way, the jagged peaks and deep canyons of the Teton Range rise straight out of the valley of Jackson Hole. The rocks at the range’s core, 2.7 billion years old, are among the oldest in North America, yet the mountains are among the youngest in the world: for about 10 million years earthquakes on the Teton fault have lifted the range while the valley floor dropped, until the same rock layers lie nearly 30,000 feet apart. Glaciers up to 3,500 feet thick flowed south from Yellowstone and filled the valley, while alpine glaciers carved the jagged skyline and left moraines that now dam lakes like Jenny Lake. The 310,000-acre park shelters some 1,200 kinds of plants, 300 of birds and more than 60 of mammals. [1]

People have used this valley for roughly 11,000 years, coming seasonally to hunt and gather because the winters were too severe to stay; permanent residents, farmers and ranchers, came only from the mid-1880s. [2] [1] Protecting it took half a century of fighting. Congress created a 96,000-acre park around the peaks and lakes on February 26, 1929. John D. Rockefeller Jr., through the Snake River Land Company, bought more than 35,000 acres of the valley floor, and in 1943 President Franklin Roosevelt proclaimed Jackson Hole National Monument — over strong local opposition, including a heavily armed cattle drive across the monument joined by the actor Wallace Beery. A compromise merged park and monument on September 14, 1950, after Rockefeller gave 32,117 acres to the nation; the HRS calls the result the culmination of 50 years of work, often marred by bitter controversy. [3]

climate.html: Only remnant glaciers remain in the Tetons, and they are shrinking. The park’s 2017 foundation document reports that its glaciers and snowfields are getting smaller each year; records show both advance and retreat, but the overall trend is retreat, and models of Wyoming’s alpine glaciers under projected climate change predict the near-complete disappearance of Teton Glacier within 30 to 75 years. A 1968 USGS map showed 9 named glaciers and about 136 smaller glaciers or perennial snowfields, but the park has never completed a thorough inventory. The same document lists glacier retreat, thinner winter snowpack and lower lake levels among the effects of climate change on the park’s scenery, and notes that landslides and avalanches are exacerbated by increasing climate variability, including more extreme events. [6] The brochure singles out whitebark pine, a keystone food source for grizzly bears and red squirrels, as sensitive to global climate change. [1]

indigenous.html:
Jackson Hole’s winters were too severe for year-round living, so for millennia its peoples came in season, following ripening plants and migrating game; the oldest buried cultural deposits in the park date to about 5,850 years ago. The mountain-dwelling people the first trappers met were Eastern Shoshone — the Tukudika, or Sheep-Eaters, who were still without horses when they were placed on the Wind River Reservation around 1868. The Shoshone still keep close ties here: in their belief system high peaks are “Power Mountain,” places to enter the spirit world through visions. [2]

Lt. Gustavus Doane, who led a near-disastrous winter expedition into Jackson Hole in 1876, is part of that history too. [4] In June 2022 Yellowstone’s Mount Doane was renamed First Peoples Mountain; the Yellowstone National Park news release announcing the change states that in 1870 Doane led an attack on a band of Piegan Blackfeet, the Marias Massacre, in which at least 173 people were killed, many of them women, elders and children sick with smallpox, and that he bragged of it for the rest of his life. [5] The Blackfeet are among the tribes Grand Teton lists as traditionally associated with the park. [6]

labor_ccc.html: When the Bureau of Reclamation dammed Jackson Lake, the shoreline trees were flooded and killed, and dead and downed trees ringed the lake. Clearing them was one of the Civilian Conservation Corps’ biggest undertakings in the valley. Young men aged 17 to 25 were stationed in camps at Leigh Lake, Lizard Point and near Colter Bay, and from 1934 at Camp NP-4 at the south end of Jenny Lake, manned through 1942. Between 1933 and 1937 they cleared the bulk of 7,000 acres of shoreline; by September 1936 crews were finishing the last 85 acres. They also built the Jenny Lake campground, trails to Phelps Lake and Garnet Canyon, telephone lines and staff housing, and several buildings from the Jenny Lake camp, meant to be temporary, were moved elsewhere and, the HRS reports, remain in use. [3]

GWMP.name: George Washington Memorial Parkway
GWMP.summary: George Washington Memorial Parkway preserves the natural scenery along the Potomac River and connects significant historic sites from Mount Vernon, George Washington's estate in Virginia, through the nation's capital. The parkway was authorized by Congress in 1930 as a memorial to the first president and was designed as a scenic and recreational corridor. The park system encompasses over 7,000 acres across multiple sites in Virginia, Maryland, and the District of Columbia, including Great Falls Park, Theodore Roosevelt Island, the Claude Moore Colonial Farm site, and the historic town of Glen Echo. The parkway itself follows part of the route Washington traveled between his Mount Vernon plantation and what would become the federal city.

HAFE.summary:
At Harpers Ferry the Potomac River cuts through the Blue Ridge and takes in the Shenandoah, leaving a V-shaped water gap that Thomas Jefferson called perhaps one of the most stupendous scenes in nature, worth a voyage across the Atlantic. That gap made the place a crossroads from the earliest human habitation onward: American Indians first, then European settlers, and in 1747 Robert Harper’s ferry across the Potomac. Congress authorized a federal armory here on June 15, 1796; when production began in 1801 it was the nation’s second, and in its workshops new ideas about interchangeable parts were tried and tested while large-scale manufacturing turned a quiet rural village into one of the leading industrial centers of its day. [1] [2]

In October 1859 John Brown and his followers seized the armory, determined to arm enslaved people and spark a rebellion; the raid failed, but his trial and execution, in the park brochure’s words, propelled the nation toward civil war. Harpers Ferry then changed hands eight times, and in September 1862 Stonewall Jackson captured nearly 12,700 Union soldiers here — the largest surrender of U.S. troops in the war. After it, Storer College opened on Camp Hill in 1867 as a school primarily for formerly enslaved people, and in 1906 hosted the Niagara Movement, where W. E. B. Du Bois laid out a demand for full civil rights. Congress authorized Harpers Ferry National Monument in 1944; it became a national historical park in 1963 and now covers 3,745 acres in West Virginia, Maryland and Virginia. [1] [2]

black.html:
During and after the war, people escaping slavery — called “contrabands” — poured into Harpers Ferry — and by the late 1860s about 700 African Americans lived in town, double the prewar number. Freewill Baptists opened a school for refugees in the armory paymaster’s Lockwood House in 1864, and on October 2, 1867, Storer College began classes there with nineteen students. Students were bullied by local residents and at times had to be escorted into town by hired militiamen. For 25 years Storer was the only institution in West Virginia offering African Americans secondary and post-secondary education; Frederick Douglass sat on its first board of trustees. [3] [2]

In August 1906 the Niagara Movement met at Storer — its first meeting in the United States — and its members walked barefoot to John Brown’s Fort to honor him; the movement led to the founding of the NAACP in 1909. Storer closed in 1955, after the State of West Virginia withdrew its support. [3] [2]

indigenous.html: People have lived in the Shenandoah and Potomac valleys since the Paleoindian period, roughly 11,000 to 9,600 B.C. A 1989–1990 excavation in Lower Town recovered 1,585 artifacts — ceramics, stone tools, postholes and hearths — from Late Archaic and Early Woodland occupations around 1200 to 500 B.C. By the time Europeans arrived about 1600, the valley had held no permanent villages for nearly a century; Tuscarora and Shawnee people lived there in temporary settlements, and Iroquois raiding parties used it as a road south. The 1744 Treaty of Lancaster, in which the Iroquois sold their land claims to the Virginia colony, pushed Native nations west of the Alleghenies. The 2017 ethnographic overview found no federally recognized tribes in the vicinity, and acknowledges that the park has devoted more of its resources to the town’s historic remains than to its pre-contact past. [3]

sources.title: Bailey, Ethnographic Overview and Assessment Study of Harpers Ferry NHP (NPS, 2017), ch. 2, Native American Presence, pp. 15–18

labor_ccc.html: The armory began in 1801 with 28 armorers who turned out 293 flintlock muskets that year; by 1810 it employed almost 200 workers in 28 buildings. Its early gunsmiths were craftsmen who built whole locks or stocks by hand and were paid by the piece, and the Ordnance Department’s campaign to impose factory discipline met fierce resistance. When Superintendent Thomas Dunn posted strict rules and inspections that cut piece-work wages, a dismissed worker, Ebenezer Cox, murdered him in his office in 1830 — and, the park’s 2006 study says, became a folk hero to the armorers. In 1842, after Major Henry Craig imposed a fixed workday enforced by a clock, the entire workforce struck for a week and sent a delegation to President John Tyler protesting that they were being made into “mere machines of labor.” Instead Congress placed military superintendents over all U.S. armories. [4]

sources.title: Lee, The U.S. Armory at Harpers Ferry: Historic Resource Study (NPS, 2006), pp. 12, 23, 29, 42–43

slavery.html:
Harpers Ferry sat in Jefferson County, Virginia, which before 1863 held twice as many enslaved people as any other county in present-day West Virginia: 4,157 in 1840, 4,341 in 1850, and 27 percent of the population by 1860. Most local owners held one or two people; the 2017 ethnographic overview records that people were bought and sold frequently, that an 1857 Charles Town court sale auctioned free Black people for remaining in the state contrary to law, and that escapes toward Pennsylvania were common enough that the Virginia Slave Insurance Company was formed to insure against them. [3]

On October 16, 1859, Brown led 21 men against an arsenal holding 100,000 arms. The first man killed was Heyward Shepherd, an African American baggage handler for the B&O Railroad. By noon the next day, the park’s own 2006 armory study records, drunken vigilantes encircled the armory and several captured raiders were brutally executed; U.S. Marines took Brown at daybreak on October 18. [3] [4]

HOBE.name: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park
HOBE.summary: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park in east-central Alabama preserves the site of the decisive battle of the Creek War. On March 27, 1814, forces led by General Andrew Jackson, including U.S. Army regulars, Tennessee militia, Cherokee allies, and Lower Creek warriors, attacked the fortified camp of the Red Stick Creek faction at a horseshoe-shaped bend on the Tallapoosa River. Approximately 800 of the 1,000 Red Stick warriors were killed in the battle — one of the deadliest defeats suffered by Native Americans in U.S. history. The resulting Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Creek Nation to cede roughly 23 million acres — half of present-day Alabama and part of southern Georgia — to the United States. The park was established in 1956.

HUTR.summary:
Hubbell Trading Post sits at 6,325 feet beside the Pueblo Colorado Wash on the edge of Ganado, Arizona, in a valley the Navajo call Lók’aah niteel, Wide Reeds, and in the middle of the Navajo Nation. People lived along this wash long before any trader: Wide Reed Ruin, a pueblo with kivas and plazas inside the site, was built in A.D. 1276–77 by tree-ring dating, and, by the administrative history’s account, the general area was largely abandoned about 1300 because of a drought that had begun in the 1270s. [1] [1] [1]

John Lorenzo Hubbell, born in Pajarito, New Mexico Territory, in 1853, began trading in the Ganado valley in 1876 and, by the park’s administrative history and foundation document, bought a trading post on this spot — William Leonard’s, the administrative history says — in 1878 (the 2010 park brochure dates the purchase to 1876). He came as the Navajo struggled to adjust to reservation life after the Long Walk. In 1883 he built a new post of uncoursed sandstone, today divided into a bullpen store, jewelry room and rug room beside a wareroom, and a U.S. post office opened there in the 1880s. At various times Hubbell and his sons owned more than 30 trading posts. He died in 1930 and lies in an unmarked grave on Hubbell Hill, following Navajo custom. [1] [1] [1]

Congress authorized the historic site on August 28, 1965, on the understanding that it would stay a working business, and Dorothy Hubbell sold it to the Park Service in 1967. It is the oldest continuously operating trading post in the Southwest: artisans still bring in rugs, jewelry, pottery and baskets, neighbors still buy groceries, and the museum collection holds more than 450,000 items. [1] [1]

indigenous.html:
In 1864 the U.S. Army forced more than 8,500 Diné (Navajo) on the Long Walk to Hwééldi — Bosque Redondo, at Fort Sumner, New Mexico Territory — for four years of imprisonment. When they came home in 1868 their hogans, herds and crops were gone, and many came to depend on traders for food. The Navajo leader Totsonii Hastiin, Ganado Mucho, invited Hubbell to the valley; when smallpox swept the reservation in 1886 Hubbell turned his home into a hospital. Traders wrote letters and served as pawnbroker and banker; the Manchesters’ 1993 administrative history counts them among the most important acculturating forces in Navajo history. [1] [1] [1] [1] [1]

The park brochure says Navajo learned weaving from Spanish, Mexican and Pueblo weavers and surpassed them, and dates blankets of Spanish Churro-sheep wool to the 1650s; Navajo-Churro ewes still lamb at the post each spring. Hubbell urged weavers toward older patterns in gray, black, white and red, the style now called Ganado Red. Daghaa Neezi, Friday Kinlicheenie, came to work at the post around 1915, kept its garden for some 70 years and, as a medicine man, performed a Blessing Way there. [1] [1] [1]

latino.html: Hubbell came from a Hispanic New Mexican family on his mother’s side. His father, James Lawrence Hubbell, came from Connecticut; his mother, Julianita Gutierrez (so spelled in the administrative history; the park brochure has “Gutierriez”), was of Spanish descent. He worked as a clerk and Spanish interpreter at forts and trading posts before he traded, married Lina Rubi of Cebolleta, New Mexico Territory, in 1879, and was known to local Hispanics as Don Lorenzo — “Don,” the administrative history notes, being a Spanish term of respect — and to the Navajo as Naakaii Sani, Old Mexican. [1] [1]

women.html: Born Dorothy Elizabeth Smith in Indiana, Dorothy Hubbell came west in 1920 to teach the Hubbell children and soon married their widowed father, Roman. By 1957, with Roman gradually paralyzed by strokes and the family company in bankruptcy, she was running the post while caring for him. That July she asked the Museum of Northern Arizona whether it could acquire and preserve the place; it could not, but the administrative history dates the movement for a national historic site to that year. She was appalled when one prospective buyer said he would sell off the contents and put in a liquor store, and the Manchesters credit her “vision, determination, and patience” for bringing the collection to the American people intact. [1] [1] [1]

INDE.summary:
Independence National Historical Park covers more than 51 acres of downtown Philadelphia, and at its center stands the old Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall. In its Assembly Room the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776; four days later the Declaration was read aloud to the public for the first time in the square outside. In 1787 fifty-five delegates were sent to Philadelphia, and in the same Assembly Room they created the Constitution — a document, the park’s own brochure says, that failed to adequately address slavery. Congress sat in nearby Congress Hall from 1790 to 1800, while Philadelphia was the nation’s capital, and the First Continental Congress had gathered at nearby Carpenters’ Hall in 1774. [1] [1]

The bell that hung in the State House steeple was first heard in 1753; its inscription reads “Proclaim Liberty throughout All the land unto All the Inhabitants Thereof.” In the 1830s anti-slavery groups named it the Liberty Bell; it cracked around 1846. The park’s brochure calls the crack a reminder that liberty is imperfect, hopefully evolving to include those denied full participation. [1] [1]

Congress created the park on June 28, 1948. The park was made by creating public parks and open green space around the founding-era landmarks, clearing later commercial buildings, drawing on the City Beautiful movement and the colonial revival of Williamsburg, and in the 1950s and 1960s park architects, archeologists and historians working on Independence Hall developed restoration methods the Park Service still treats as a model. Independence Hall was named a World Heritage Site in 1979. [1] [1] [1]

black.html: Ona Judge hid among the free Black Philadelphians she had befriended — part of a city the brochure describes as home to people fleeing slavery and free people of African descent. The house itself was torn down in 1832, and for some fifty years after Independence Mall was built the site lay under a lawn and a women’s restroom, marked only by a small brass plaque. In 2002 independent scholar Edward Lawler Jr. showed that Washington had ordered a smokehouse on the lot altered as housing for his “stablepeople.” Lawler judged it most likely that the order was carried out and the building housed enslaved stable workers, and he pointed out that visitors would pass over that site on entering the new Liberty Bell Center; in the controversy that followed, attorney Michael Coard founded the Avenging the Ancestors Coalition, and on July 3, 2002, some five hundred mostly African American protesters demanded a memorial. The 2007 excavation uncovered the kitchen where Hercules cooked and drew more than 300,000 visitors in four months; the park then built its first community-based exhibit there, interpreting race and slavery. [1] [1] [1]

slavery.html: Partly beneath today’s Liberty Bell Center stood the President’s House, the executive mansion of George Washington (1790–1797) and John Adams (1797–1800). The Washingtons brought nine enslaved Africans from Mount Vernon to work there at various times: Austin, Christopher Sheels, Giles, Hercules, Joe Richardson, Moll, Ona (Oney) Judge, Paris and Richmond. Under Pennsylvania’s Gradual Abolition Law of 1780, the park’s 2009 excavation report (revised 2023) explains, enslaved people became free after a six-month stay in the state, so Washington rotated them back to Virginia — a practice the report says itself violated Pennsylvania law, which was not enforced. In the spring of 1796 Ona Judge walked out while the family sat down to dinner and escaped to New Hampshire; she died free in 1848. Hercules, the chef, escaped from Mount Vernon on February 22, 1797. Adams, the brochure notes, never owned slaves. [1] [1]

women.html: Lucretia Mott and other activists of the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society wrote for The Liberty Bell, the Boston abolitionist annual that in 1839 first gave the bell its name in print and for twenty years used it as an anti-slavery symbol, John Paige’s special history study for the park records. On July 4, 1876, Susan B. Anthony gave the first public reading of a women’s declaration of rights here, urging suffrage. And on August 2, 1954, the General Federation of Women’s Clubs gave the Park Service $209,541.82 raised nationwide to restore and refurnish the first floor of Independence Hall — by the park’s account the largest single sum ever applied to the building to that time. [1] [1] [1]

INDU.name: Indiana Dunes National Park (National Lakeshore)
INDU.summary: Indiana Dunes National Park on the southern shore of Lake Michigan in northwestern Indiana protects 15,349 acres of dunes, wetlands, prairies, rivers, and forests. The park's origins trace to the early 20th-century conservation campaign led by botanist Henry Cowles, whose groundbreaking studies of plant succession on the Indiana dunes helped establish the modern science of ecology. Despite being surrounded by one of the most heavily industrialized regions in North America, the park supports remarkable biodiversity — over 1,100 native plant species, the fourth-highest count of any national park unit. Originally designated as Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore in 1966, it was redesignated as a national park in 2019.

JELA.summary:
The Mississippi River built this country. At the end of its journey it drops sediment scoured from 40 percent of the continental United States, and the ground beneath the New Orleans region is less than 4,000 years old — marsh, slow bayous, cypress swamp and forested natural levees in a restless interplay of land and water. American Indians settled the delta as it formed, some 2,500 years ago; from the 1720s European settlers and enslaved Africans took their place among them, and the park’s brochure traces how French, Chitimacha and Houma, West African, Spanish-speaking Isleño, Caribbean and Acadian peoples together made the culture now called Creole and Cajun. [1]

On January 8, 1815, on the Chalmet plantation below New Orleans, Andrew Jackson’s mixed force of regulars, militia, volunteers and Jean Lafitte’s Baratarian privateers stopped a British assault in less than two hours; more than 2,000 British soldiers were killed, wounded or captured and American casualties numbered fewer than 20. Chalmette National Historical Park, created in 1939 to preserve part of that field, was the first national park unit in Louisiana. Congress expanded it into Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve on November 10, 1978, and in 1988 added three Acadian cultural centers, for six sites in all. The land itself is now going: blocked sedimentation, subsidence and rising seas cost the delta, by the brochure’s count, a football field’s worth of land every 45 minutes. [1] [2]

black.html: Around 1867, Jean Pierre Fazende, a free man of color before emancipation, began selling lots on part of the old Chalmet plantation to freedmen. Fazendeville grew into a close-knit Black working-class village of about 40 houses, a church, stores, a school and benevolent societies, sitting between the battlefield monument and the national cemetery, which for generations drew its laborers from the village. Blythe’s 2012 administrative history records that NPS managers believed from the start that the community would have to be obliterated to restore the historic scene. Congress authorized purchase of every property in 1962, and by 1964 the village was gone — taken, former residents told an anthropologist, while Black residents of St. Bernard Parish were still fighting for the vote. The same history notes that park managers long overlooked the free men of color who fought for Jackson. The NPS placed a wayside about Fazendeville on the battlefield in 2008. [3] [2]

sources.title: Blythe, Administrative History of Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve (NPS, 2012), ch. 3 pp. 35–36; ch. 4 pp. 57–58

climate.html: The delta was always in motion: over 3,500 years the Mississippi built five major deltas, the newest only 500 years old, while subsidence and erosion balanced the new land it laid down. Levees and channelization have broken that balance. The park’s 2015 foundation document says parts of this landscape have the highest rate of relative sea-level rise and land loss in North America — a historical average of 0.36 inches a year at Grand Isle from 1947 to 2012, with projections for 2100 of 3.3 to 7.6 feet. In Barataria Preserve, scientists have already documented species lost from the natural levee ridges, more flooding and land loss, and the document names the climate-driven rise of ocean influence over the delta and its people the park’s major cross-cutting concern. [1] [2]

indigenous.html: People lived in the Barataria basin as soon as the river formed it, and by the Marksville period (about 100 B.C. to A.D. 300) were building large villages, growing corn and probably beans and squash while relying chiefly on hunting, fishing and gathering. Prehistoric shell middens from that long occupation remain part of the preserve’s landscape. At French contact their descendants were the Washa, Chawasha and Chitimacha (“Sitimachas” on a 1718 French map). France’s Indian allies waged a twelve-year war on the Chitimacha which, Holmes writes, supplied the French colony with many Indian slaves from Chitimacha bands; the 1718 peace forced the Chitimacha to abandon Bayou Lafourche and settle near New Orleans. By 1739 the Washa and Chawasha together numbered only thirty warriors, a collapse the study attributes probably to disease. [4] [2]

latino.html: Spain ruled Louisiana from 1763 to 1800, and its colonial government built the road through the preserve still called El Camino Real de Barataria, the royal road. In 1778 the first settlers from the Canary Islands — the Isleños — arrived, brought by the Spanish governor to strengthen Spain’s hold against British and American aggression. In 1779 a group of about 150 settled at the meeting of Bayou des Familles and Bayou Barataria; the bayou’s name, “of the families,” comes from them. Hurricanes and river crevasses wore the settlement down over some sixteen years, until a crevasse that opened in or before 1796 ruined the last five families’ crops and livestock and the government moved them to Terre aux Boeufs, in today’s St. Bernard Parish. [1] [2] [4]

slavery.html: The Barataria basin south of New Orleans was sugar country before the Civil War. In 1850, Holmes’s 1986 historic resource study counts 1,176 people living there: 504 enslaved, 15 free people of color and 657 white, with 79 percent of the enslaved owned by planters and living on the plantations. In 1856 the Mavis Grove plantation inventoried houses for 156 enslaved people alongside its steam sawmill, seventy mules and $226,914 in total value. Enslaved workers labored six days a week, and every day during the October-to-December harvest and grinding season. Jean Lafitte’s smuggling empire in the basin, which the park’s foundation document notes trafficked in enslaved people, was bold enough to advertise auctions of contraband slaves openly. [4] [2]

LOWE.name: Lowell National Historical Park
LOWE.summary: Lowell National Historical Park in Lowell, Massachusetts, preserves and interprets the history of America's Industrial Revolution in the nation's first large-scale planned industrial city. In the 1820s, a group of Boston investors known as the Boston Manufacturing Company built a network of power canals and textile mills along the Merrimack River, creating a factory system that transformed American manufacturing. The mills employed thousands of young women — known as the "mill girls" — who left New England farms to work in the factories, representing one of the first large-scale entries of American women into the industrial workforce. The park was established in 1978 and preserves 5.6 miles of canals, operating gatehouses, and mill buildings in a model of urban industrial heritage preservation.

MACA.name: Mammoth Cave National Park
MACA.summary: Mammoth Cave National Park in central Kentucky protects the world's longest known cave system, with over 420 miles of surveyed passageways — more than twice the length of any other known cave. The cave was formed over millions of years as mildly acidic water dissolved the park's thick limestone bedrock. Native Americans explored and mined minerals in the cave at least 4,000 years ago, and during the War of 1812, enslaved laborers were forced to mine calcium nitrate (saltpeter) from the cave for use in gunpowder. Enslaved men, most notably Stephen Bishop, served as the cave's first guides in the 1830s and 1840s, making major explorations and mapping discoveries. The park was established in 1941 and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981 and an International Biosphere Reserve in 1990.

MANA.name: Manassas National Battlefield Park
MANA.summary: Manassas National Battlefield Park in Prince William County, Virginia, preserves the site of two major Civil War battles. The First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) on July 21, 1861, was the war's first major land engagement, shattering both sides' expectations of a quick conflict and earning Confederate General Thomas J. Jackson his famous nickname "Stonewall." The Second Battle of Manassas, fought August 28–30, 1862, was a decisive Confederate victory that brought Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia to the doorstep of Washington, D.C. and set the stage for Lee's first invasion of the North. The battlefield was designated a national battlefield park in 1940 and preserves approximately 5,000 acres of the historic landscape.

MEMY.name: Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument
MEMY.summary: Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument in Jackson, Mississippi, preserves the modest ranch-style house where civil rights leader Medgar Evers lived with his wife Myrlie and their three children. Evers served as the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi, organizing voter registration drives, economic boycotts, and investigations into racial violence during the height of the civil rights movement. On June 12, 1963, Evers was assassinated in his driveway by white supremacist Byron De La Beckwith — a murder that galvanized the civil rights movement and contributed to the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The site was designated a national monument by President Barack Obama in 2020. Myrlie Evers-Williams went on to become a prominent civil rights leader in her own right, serving as chair of the NAACP.

MONO.name: Monocacy National Battlefield
MONO.summary: Monocacy National Battlefield near Frederick, Maryland, preserves the site of the Battle of Monocacy, fought on July 9, 1864 — often called "The Battle That Saved Washington." When Confederate General Jubal Early led an army toward the Union capital, a hastily assembled force of Union soldiers under General Lew Wallace (later the author of "Ben-Hur") delayed Early's advance for an entire day at the Monocacy River crossing. Although the Union forces were defeated, the delay allowed reinforcements to reach Washington's defenses in time to prevent the capital's capture. The battlefield was established as a national battlefield in 1934 and preserves 1,647 acres of agricultural landscape and historic structures.

MORA.summary:
Mount Rainier is the tallest volcano in the Cascade Range and the most heavily glaciated peak in the continental United States, a 14,410-foot mountain whose rivers of ice run up to 750 feet deep while steam still escapes from vents at its summit. Below the ice the seasons are compressed: in the subalpine meadows summer may last only two months, and the wildflowers, insects, birds and mammals race through it before the snow returns. [1]

Archaeological findings suggest people have been coming to the mountain for more than 9,000 years. Congress made it the nation’s fifth national park on March 2, 1899, and in 1988 designated more than 97 percent of it as wilderness. Nearly two million people a year now walk its meadows and old-growth forest and sleep in rustic log-and-boulder lodges built a century ago, in a landscape the Park Service itself calls anything but permanent: ice and rock break away from the peak, rivers of meltwater and debris wreak havoc with roads and buildings, and the brochure handed to visitors concedes that as the planet warms, no one knows how the mountain’s plants, animals or visitors will fare. [1]

climate.html: The Nisqually Glacier, visible from the road to Paradise, has been watched longer than almost any glacier in America: its terminus was first recorded in 1857, and it has since retreated more than two and a quarter kilometres up the mountain. Weather stations at Longmire and Paradise show the forty-five years from 1970 to 2015 growing 1.5 °C warmer and 0.77 metres drier, and the glacier losing another 280 metres of length in that span; researchers expect it to keep shrinking unless the climate changes. The ice does not go quietly. Ten outburst floods have surged from the glacier in the period of record, nine of them during retreat, sending water and rock down the Nisqually toward the park’s roads and buildings. [4] [5]

indigenous.html:
Long before it was a park, the mountain was a late-summer destination. The ethnographer Allan H. Smith, whose 1960s fieldwork Catton reports (and partly questions), identified five peoples who used it — the Nisqually, Puyallup, Muckleshoot, Yakima (today’s Yakama Nation) and Taidnapam: families climbed from the lowland valleys and over the passes to camp in the high meadows when the huckleberries ripened, to hunt deer, elk and mountain goat, and occasionally to seek spirit power. Each fall they set fire to the meadows so the berry patches would spread — a practice park officials never understood and never continued. Early accounts rendered the mountain’s name as “Takhoma,” though Catton cautions that much of what settlers wrote about Indian belief was shaped to suit their own purposes. [2] [3]

The treaties of 1854 and 1855 that ceded this country reserved the privilege of hunting and gathering roots and berries on “open and unclaimed land,” but after 1899 park officials treated the mountain as closed. In 1915 the Interior Department’s solicitor concluded that the treaty right had survived the park’s creation; a year later the Park Service’s chief clerk advised that state law and two court decisions had superseded that opinion, and rangers kept enforcing the ban. In October 1917 six Yakima people — four men and two women, by the newspaper account Catton quotes — were arrested at Yakima Park with freshly skinned deer hides and fined. Catton’s conclusion is that the park amplified and distorted Indian legends at the same time as it altered Indian use of the mountain. Descendants of those nations still hold the mountain as a place of special connection today. [2] [1]

labor_ccc.html: Much of what visitors still touch at Rainier — the stone guardrails, log cabins and campgrounds — was built by young men of the Depression. By mid-July 1933 more than a thousand Civilian Conservation Corps enrollees, single men aged 18 to 25 from families on relief, were at work in five park camps; many companies were shipped west by train, including three from New York and one from Illinois in the first season and, in 1937, a company of 140 from Arkansas. One crew spent 703 man-days on a single mile of trail past Narada Falls. The Corps was segregated nationally: Black enrollees were underrepresented and mostly formed into separate companies, and Native Americans were enrolled in a separate Indian Division that worked on reservations. Public Works Administration money nominally outspent the CCC, CWA and WPA combined at Rainier — a figure Catton calls deceiving, since much of it continued the 1920s road program — but it is the Corps’ log cabins, stone comfort stations and stone guardrails that Catton calls its most enduring legacy. [7]

sources.title: Catton, Wonderland (1996), ch. 11, The Impact of the New Deal

women.html: On the afternoon of August 10, 1890, Fay Fuller, a nineteen-year-old Tacoma schoolteacher, stood on the summit in ankle-length bloomers after a two-day climb with four men — the first woman known to have reached the top. Three summers earlier a party had let her come along only on condition that she turn back at 8,500 feet; she went home resolved to go as high as she could. Guide Leonard Longmire, remembering her in 1933, said she rode astride rather than sidesaddle and drilled with rifles alongside a group of young Tacoma women who called themselves the Women’s Guard — behaviour, Potts suggests, that drew criticism from townspeople. Her published account drew fresh attention to the mountain and to mountaineering, particularly for women. [6]

MORR.name: Morristown National Historical Park
MORR.summary: Morristown National Historical Park in Morristown, New Jersey, was the first national historical park in the United States, established on March 2, 1933. The park preserves sites associated with two critical winter encampments of the Continental Army during the American Revolution. During the winter of 1779–1780, General George Washington quartered his army of approximately 10,000 soldiers at Jockey Hollow, where they endured what was recorded as the coldest winter of the 18th century — with 28 snowstorms and temperatures colder than at Valley Forge. Washington used the nearby Ford Mansion as his headquarters. The park also preserves Fort Nonsense and the New Jersey Brigade encampment area.

MUWO.name: Muir Woods National Monument
MUWO.summary: Muir Woods National Monument in Marin County, California, protects 554 acres of old-growth coast redwood forest in a sheltered valley on the Pacific coast just north of San Francisco. The monument was established by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 after Congressman William Kent and his wife Elizabeth Thacher Kent purchased the land to save it from logging and donated it to the federal government. Kent requested that the monument be named in honor of naturalist John Muir, who called it "the best tree-lovers monument that could possibly be found in all the forests of the world." Some of the redwood trees in the monument are over 250 feet tall and more than 1,000 years old. The monument is part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site component in the Redwood National and State Parks serial nomination.
