NAMA.summary:
For more than two centuries the National Mall — the great green swath that runs from the foot of the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River — has been the nation’s premier civic and symbolic space. National Mall and Memorial Parks cares for it and more than 1,000 acres of parkland across Washington: the Washington Monument and the Lincoln, Jefferson, Roosevelt, King, Korean War, Vietnam Veterans, World War I and World War II memorials, Ford’s Theatre, Pennsylvania Avenue, and more than 150 circles, squares and small reservations, from the African American Civil War Memorial to Logan Circle. [1] [2]

Its open spaces are as old as the capital: Pierre L’Enfant’s 1791 plan, commissioned by President Washington, laid them out as a stage for remembrance, celebration and the exercise of First Amendment rights, and federal review bodies are still charged with protecting both it and the 1901 McMillan Plan. For decades the federal government largely neglected the Mall itself; after its oak forest was cleared in the 1810s it became eroded scrubland where pigs and cows grazed. The parks passed to the National Park Service in 1933, and today they draw more than 33 million visitors a year to a place that, in the Park Service’s words, hosts history in the making — from presidential inaugurals to civil rights demonstrations. [2] [3]

black.html: In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let the African American opera singer Marian Anderson sing at Constitution Hall, which kept a White-performers-only policy; the segregated D.C. school board also turned her away. Organizers turned instead to the Lincoln Memorial, and Interior Secretary Harold Ickes, whose Park Service managed it, handled most of the arrangements. On Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, Anderson sang from the memorial’s steps to an integrated crowd of 75,000 that stretched toward the Washington Monument. The study quotes historian Scott Sandage’s judgment that with the concert the civil rights movement began to develop a strategy of mass, symbolic protest. On August 28, 1963, more than 200,000 people marched from the Washington Monument to the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom; Anderson opened it with the national anthem, and Martin Luther King Jr. delivered “I Have a Dream.” [3]

sources.title: Events and Celebrations on the National Mall HRS (NPS, 2024), ch. 'The Making of a Political and Protest Space (1930–1963)', PDF pp. 208–219

climate.html: Part of the park sits on ground taken from the river: West and East Potomac parks were built on reclaimed land, and the 2017 foundation document reports that the seawalls built to keep the water out are crumbling and failing. Both parks remain vulnerable to river flooding and sea level rise even with portions of the Potomac Park levee completed; the park’s own headquarters lay below the normal high tide line, where high water had become a regular occurrence, and the area around the Tidal Basin is a major concern. The document expects the problem to be made worse by climate change’s effects on sea level and storm surges, and calls it a critical issue for the park. [2]

sources.title: Foundation Document, National Mall and Memorial Parks (2017) — Key Issues: Climate Change, Environmental Impacts, and Sea Level Rise, PDF p. 37

slavery.html: In the early nineteenth century, the 2024 historic resource study notes, the horror of American slavery was on full display on the Mall: pens holding enslaved people stood at its edge at 7th Street NW, and coffles of enslaved men and women, chained together, were marched across it to the loading docks on the Potomac. [3] North of the Mall, at Vermont Avenue and U Street NW, the African American Civil War Memorial honors the more than 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors who served in the U.S. Army and Navy during the Civil War — service that, the foundation document says, helped end the war and free more than four million enslaved people. The memorial’s curved walls carry the names of the men who served. [2]

sources.title: Events and Celebrations on the National Mall HRS (NPS, 2024), ch. 1 — early nineteenth-century Mall, PDF p. 42
Foundation Document, National Mall and Memorial Parks (2017) — African American Civil War Memorial description

women.html: On March 3, 1913, the day before Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration, the National American Woman Suffrage Association’s Woman Suffrage Procession, organized by Alice Paul and Lucy Burns, marched down Pennsylvania Avenue from the Capitol toward the Treasury. A crowd of about 250,000 spilled into the street; men heckled, spat on and assaulted the marchers while police proved unable or unwilling to control them. The protests kept coming. Paul and Burns joined Alva Belmont in founding the National Woman’s Party in 1916, and through 1917 more than 1,000 women picketed the White House; between June and November police arrested 218 of them for “obstructing sidewalk traffic.” Wilson signaled support for the suffrage amendment in January 1918, and the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. The Park Service’s 2024 study credits the 1913 march with further establishing Washington as a national stage for large-scale demonstration. [3]

sources.title: Events and Celebrations on the National Mall HRS (NPS, 2024), Woman Suffrage Procession section, PDF pp. 197–199

NATR.name: Natchez Trace Parkway
NATR.summary: The Natchez Trace Parkway is a 444-mile scenic road that follows the approximate route of the historic Natchez Trace, an ancient travel corridor connecting Natchez, Mississippi, to Nashville, Tennessee. The original trace was used for thousands of years by Native Americans, including the Natchez, Chickasaw, and Choctaw nations, and became a major route for "Kaintuck" boatmen who floated goods down the Mississippi River to Natchez or New Orleans and then walked home overland. The trace's peak use was between 1785 and 1820, before steamboats made the return trip upriver practical. The parkway, administered by the National Park Service, was authorized in 1938 and substantially completed in 2005, passing through diverse landscapes from cypress swamps to Appalachian foothills.

NRSS.name: Natural Resource Stewardship
NRSS.summary: The National Park Service's natural resource stewardship mission dates to the agency's founding in 1916, when the Organic Act charged the NPS with conserving "the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein" for the enjoyment of future generations. The NPS Natural Resource Stewardship and Science Directorate oversees programs in biological resources, geologic resources, water resources, air quality, climate change science, and inventory and monitoring across more than 400 park units. These scientific programs produce peer-reviewed research that informs park management decisions and contributes to the broader scientific understanding of ecosystem health, biodiversity, and environmental change across the nation's most protected landscapes.

ORPI.name: Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument
ORPI.summary: Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in southwestern Arizona protects 330,689 acres of Sonoran Desert wilderness along the U.S.–Mexico border — the only place in the United States where the organ pipe cactus grows wild. Proclaimed a national monument in 1937, the park was designated a UNESCO International Biosphere Reserve in 1976 in recognition of its outstanding desert ecosystem biodiversity. The monument harbors 28 species of cactus, over 270 species of birds, and rare mammals including the Sonoran pronghorn, one of the most endangered land mammals in North America. The Tohono O'odham people have lived in and around the monument's lands for centuries and maintain cultural connections to the landscape. The monument's location on the international border has made it a focal point in immigration and border security debates.

PETE.name: Petersburg National Battlefield
PETE.summary: Petersburg National Battlefield in Virginia preserves the sites associated with the Siege of Petersburg, a nine-month campaign from June 1864 to April 1865 that ultimately led to the end of the Civil War. General Ulysses S. Grant's strategy to cut the vital railroad supply lines feeding the Confederate capital at Richmond resulted in one of the war's longest sustained operations, with miles of trenches foreshadowing the trench warfare of World War I. The siege included the Battle of the Crater on July 30, 1864, in which Union forces detonated a mine beneath Confederate lines — an assault that ended in a disastrous Union defeat and particularly heavy casualties among United States Colored Troops. The fall of Petersburg on April 2, 1865, led directly to the evacuation of Richmond and Lee's surrender at Appomattox a week later.

REER.name: Reconstruction Era Historical Park (National Monument)
REER.summary: Reconstruction Era National Historical Park in Beaufort County, South Carolina, was established in 2017 as the first unit of the National Park System dedicated to the Reconstruction era (1861–1900). The park preserves sites in and around Beaufort associated with the transition from slavery to freedom, including the Brick Baptist Church — where formerly enslaved people first learned to read — and the Darrah Hall at Penn Center, one of the first schools for freed African Americans in the South. The Sea Islands of South Carolina were among the earliest places where the federal government experimented with programs for formerly enslaved people, including land redistribution, education, and political participation. The park tells the stories of newly freed people who built schools, churches, and communities and exercised their rights as citizens during this transformative period.

RIRA.name: River Raisin National Battlefield Park
RIRA.summary: River Raisin National Battlefield Park in Monroe, Michigan, preserves the site of the January 1813 battles that were among the deadliest engagements of the War of 1812 on American soil. On January 22, 1813, a combined British and Native American force defeated a larger American army along the River Raisin, and the following day, wounded American prisoners were killed in what became known as the River Raisin Massacre — the deadliest single event for U.S. forces in the war. The rallying cry "Remember the Raisin!" became a powerful recruiting tool for the American war effort. The park was designated a national battlefield park in 2010, making it the 392nd unit of the National Park System and the only national battlefield park dedicated to the War of 1812.

ROCR.name: Rock Creek Park
ROCR.summary: Rock Creek Park in Washington, D.C., is one of the largest and oldest urban parks in the United States. Established by an act of Congress in 1890 — just two years after Yellowstone — the park preserves nearly 1,800 acres of forested valley along Rock Creek and its tributaries in the heart of the nation's capital. The park was created to protect the creek's watershed and provide a natural retreat for city residents during the rapid urbanization of late 19th-century Washington. Rock Creek Park includes the Civil War-era Fort DeRussy, Peirce Mill (a 19th-century grist mill), and significant archaeological sites with evidence of Native American habitation dating back thousands of years. The park's forests, trails, and Nature Center make it a vital green space in one of the country's most densely developed metropolitan areas.

SAAN.name: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park
SAAN.summary: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park in San Antonio, Texas, preserves four of the five Spanish colonial missions established along the San Antonio River in the 18th century: Mission Concepción, Mission San José, Mission San Juan, and Mission Espada. Together with the Alamo (Mission San Antonio de Valero), these missions represent the largest concentration of Spanish colonial missions in North America. Founded between 1718 and 1731 by Franciscan friars, the missions served as centers for converting and acculturating Native American peoples into Spanish colonial society. The park was established in 1978 and the missions were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 — the first World Heritage Site in Texas — recognized for their outstanding example of the interchange of Spanish and Coahuiltecan cultures.

SAJH.name: San Juan Island National Historical Park
SAJH.summary: San Juan Island National Historical Park in Washington State preserves the sites of the 1859 Pig War confrontation between the United States and Great Britain over possession of the San Juan Islands. The dispute began when an American settler shot a British-owned pig and escalated into a military standoff with both nations deploying forces on the island. The conflict was resolved through 12 years of joint military occupation and ultimately settled by international arbitration in 1872, when Kaiser Wilhelm I of Germany ruled in favor of the United States. The park preserves both the American Camp and English Camp — the respective military installations — and the island's prairie, forest, and shoreline ecosystems. The park was established in 1966.

SAND.name: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site
SAND.summary: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site in southeastern Colorado preserves the location where, on November 29, 1864, approximately 675 U.S. volunteer soldiers attacked a peaceful encampment of Cheyenne and Arapaho people, killing an estimated 150 to 200 men, women, children, and elders. The village, led by Chiefs Black Kettle and Left Hand, had been assured of safety by U.S. military officials, and an American flag and a white flag of surrender flew over the camp during the attack. The massacre was condemned by some contemporaries, including a Congressional investigation, but no perpetrators were prosecuted. The site was designated a national historic site in 2007 after extensive consultation with descendants of the Cheyenne and Arapaho victims, who participated in identifying the massacre location.

SARI.name: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve
SARI.summary: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve on the island of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands is the only known site where members of a Columbus expedition set foot on what is now U.S. territory. On November 14, 1493, during Columbus's second voyage, a landing party encountered the Kalinago (Carib) people in Salt River Bay — the encounter turned violent and is considered the first documented armed conflict between Europeans and Native Americans. The site also preserves a ceremonial ball court and village site of the Taino people, who inhabited the island before European contact. Established as a national historical park in 1992, Salt River Bay protects one of the largest remaining mangrove forests in the Virgin Islands and a rich marine ecosystem including coral reefs, seagrass beds, and a submarine canyon.

SCBL.name: Scotts Bluff National Monument
SCBL.summary: Scotts Bluff National Monument in western Nebraska preserves a prominent natural landmark along the North Platte River that served as a major waypoint on the Oregon Trail, California Trail, and Mormon Trail during the great westward migrations of the 19th century. The bluff, rising 800 feet above the river valley, was visible for miles and marked the passage through a gap in the series of steep bluffs that forced travelers to find specific routes through the terrain. An estimated 250,000 emigrants passed through Mitchell Pass at the base of the bluff between the 1840s and 1860s, and deep wagon wheel ruts are still visible today. The monument was established in 1919 and includes a museum with one of the finest collections of watercolors by pioneer artist William Henry Jackson.

SEMO.name: Selma to Montgomery NHT
SEMO.summary: The Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail in Alabama traces the 54-mile route of the 1965 Voting Rights marches from Selma to the state capital in Montgomery — a watershed moment in the American civil rights movement. The first march on March 7, 1965 — "Bloody Sunday" — ended when state and local police attacked approximately 600 peaceful marchers with billy clubs and tear gas at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, an event broadcast on national television that shocked the nation. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led a subsequent march that successfully reached Montgomery on March 25, 1965, with 25,000 supporters. The marches directly led to President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the Voting Rights Act of 1965, one of the most significant pieces of civil rights legislation in American history. The trail was designated in 1996.

SITK.name: Sitka National Historical Park
SITK.summary: Sitka National Historical Park in Sitka, Alaska, is the oldest federally designated park in Alaska, established as a public park in 1890 and redesignated a national monument in 1910 and a national historical park in 1972. The park preserves the site of the 1804 Battle of Sitka — the last major armed resistance by the Tlingit people against Russian colonization in Alaska. The battle occurred when Tlingit warriors defended a wooden fort (the Shís'gi Noow) against a combined Russian and Aleut force; after several days of fighting, the Tlingit withdrew in a strategic retreat. The park also houses the Southeast Alaska Indian Cultural Center, where Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian artists practice and demonstrate traditional carving, weaving, and other art forms, and maintains a renowned collection of totem poles along a temperate rainforest trail.

SLBE.name: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore
SLBE.summary: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore on the northeastern coast of Lake Michigan in Michigan protects 35 miles of shoreline, massive perched sand dunes rising up to 450 feet above the lake, pristine inland lakes, dense beech-maple forests, and two offshore wilderness islands — North and South Manitou. The national lakeshore was established in 1970, and in 2011 viewers of ABC's "Good Morning America" voted its beaches the "Most Beautiful Place in America." The park's name derives from a Chippewa (Ojibwe) legend in which a mother bear and her two cubs swam across Lake Michigan to escape a forest fire; the mother bear waited on the bluff for her cubs, who drowned and became the Manitou Islands, while she became the Sleeping Bear Dune. The park's diverse ecosystems support endangered piping plovers and over 100 species of migratory birds.

STRI.name: Stones River NB
STRI.summary: Stones River National Battlefield near Murfreesboro, Tennessee, preserves the site of the Battle of Stones River (also known as the Battle of Murfreesboro), fought from December 31, 1862, to January 2, 1863. The battle was among the bloodiest of the Civil War, with roughly 23,000 combined casualties — a casualty rate comparable to the Battle of Antietam. The Union victory under Major General William S. Rosecrans secured central Tennessee for the Union and provided a critical morale boost following the Confederate victory at Fredericksburg. The Stones River National Cemetery, established in 1865 at the battlefield, is the oldest national cemetery in the country established during the Civil War. The site was established as a national battlefield in 1927.

TAPR.name: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve
TAPR.summary: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in the Flint Hills of east-central Kansas protects a remnant of the tallgrass prairie ecosystem that once covered 170 million acres of North America — from Indiana to Kansas and from Canada to Texas. Less than 4 percent of the original tallgrass prairie remains today, making it one of the most endangered ecosystems on the continent, and the Flint Hills contain the largest remaining expanse. The preserve was established in 1996 through a public-private partnership between the National Park Service and The Nature Conservancy. The nearly 11,000-acre site includes the historic Spring Hill/Z Bar Ranch with an 1881 limestone ranch house, a massive stone barn, and a one-room schoolhouse. A bison herd was reintroduced to the preserve in 2009.

THRO.name: Theodore Roosevelt National Park
THRO.summary: Theodore Roosevelt National Park in the badlands of western North Dakota memorializes the 26th president and the landscape that profoundly influenced his conservation philosophy. Roosevelt first came to the Dakota Territory in 1883 to hunt bison and subsequently established two cattle ranches — the Maltese Cross and Elkhorn — in the Little Missouri River badlands. His experiences with the harsh beauty of the landscape and his witness to the decimation of wildlife and open range shaped his lifelong commitment to conservation. As president from 1901 to 1909, Roosevelt established the United States Forest Service, created 5 national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 bird reserves, and 150 national forests, protecting roughly 230 million acres. The park was designated a national memorial park in 1947 and redesignated a national park in 1978.

VICK.name: Vicksburg National Military Park
VICK.summary: Vicksburg National Military Park in Vicksburg, Mississippi, preserves the site of the decisive Civil War campaign and 47-day siege that gave the Union control of the Mississippi River. After months of failed approaches, General Ulysses S. Grant executed a brilliant campaign in the spring of 1863, crossing the river south of Vicksburg, winning five battles in 17 days, and laying siege to the city's defenses. The Confederate garrison surrendered on July 4, 1863 — one day after the Union victory at Gettysburg — and President Abraham Lincoln declared that "The Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea." The park, established in 1899, contains over 1,340 monuments, markers, and plaques; a restored Union gunboat (the USS Cairo); and the Vicksburg National Cemetery with over 17,000 Union graves.

VIIS.summary:
Just over half of the small, rugged volcanic island of St. John is protected as Virgin Islands National Park: moist forest on the interior mountains, cactus scrub on the dry south-facing slopes, white beaches at Trunk, Cinnamon and Hawksnest bays, and offshore a world of mangroves, seagrass and coral. More than 800 kinds of plants grow here, among them the teyer palm, the island’s only native palm, and the bay rum tree whose leaves once scented a famous cologne; over 50 species of tropical birds breed on the island, and hawksbill and green sea turtles feed in its waters. The reefs are slow work — the fastest corals grow two or three inches a year, and large brain corals are centuries old. [1]

Congress established the park on August 2, 1956, on land that Rockefeller interests had bought and given to the federal government. In 1962 it gained 5,650 acres of submerged lands, in 1978 128 acres on Hassel Island in St. Thomas harbor, and in 2001 a presidential proclamation created the adjoining Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument on 12,708 more acres of sea floor. The Park Service now manages almost 58 percent of St. John’s land and more than 18,000 acres underwater, and in 1976 UNESCO made the park one of the first international biosphere reserves. [1] [2]

People have lived on these islands for at least 3,000 years. The park’s cultural resources include hundreds of historic structures, and its 2016 foundation document is plain about what built the plantation landscape: a plantation economy raised under Danish rule with the forced labor of enslaved people, primarily from Africa. It names the park as a place to explore the experience of the enslaved Africans and the history of slavery in the West Indies. [2]

climate.html: In September and October 2005, after record-warm seawater, an average of 90 percent of the coral cover at the long-term monitoring sites around St. John and St. Croix bleached white. Many corals began to regain their color and were then hit by disease, chiefly white plague — what National Park Service and U.S. Geological Survey scientists called a “one-two punch.” By July 2006 coral cover at the study sites had fallen 48.7 percent, the worst coral mortality the islands had seen from any cause in 40 years; it was also the first time bleaching of elkhorn coral, listed as threatened that May, had ever been observed in the Virgin Islands. [5] The park’s 2016 foundation document records that Caribbean air temperatures rose more than one degree Fahrenheit over the past century and relative sea level is climbing about 3.9 inches per 100 years, and expects more bleaching and disease outbreaks; shoreline erosion is already damaging coastal archeological sites. [2]

indigenous.html: From St. John it is possible to sight and navigate to Puerto Rico and every island in between, to St. Croix and to all the British Virgin Islands, and the northern Virgin Islands’ cultural chronology corresponds with eastern Puerto Rico’s throughout prehistory. Kenneth Wild of Virgin Islands National Park reports that excavations at Trunk Bay and Cinnamon Bay trace a ceramic sequence beginning around AD 800, and at Cinnamon Bay a ceremonial offering place — an articulated turtle plastron, a decorated vessel of closed ark shells, a carved zemi head, shell and gold inlays for statues — preserved beneath a colonial road in use since the mid-1600s. Wild reads the change in styles around AD 1200 as a pivotal point in the development of Taíno culture. [4] The Reef Bay petroglyphs, which the 2016 foundation document counts among the best-preserved rock art in the Caribbean, were in 2016 the only one of the 22 prehistoric sites recorded on St. John listed on the National Register. The Taíno who met Columbus were decimated by European disease, enslavement and overwork under Spanish colonization. [2] [1]

slavery.html:
The Danes raised their flag at Coral Bay in 1718; by 1733 nearly all of St. John was in sugar cane and cotton, and enslaved people outnumbered Europeans 1,087 to 208. [1] [2] After drought, a hurricane and insects destroyed the food crops, many fled into the forest, and Governor Philip Gardelin answered with the 1733 Slave Code: flogging, amputation, public torture and execution. Early on November 23, 1733, Akwamu fighters with cane knives hidden in firewood seized the Danish fort at Coral Bay. Led by King Claes, King Juni and Kanta, they fought for six months, until about 400 French soldiers came from Martinique; many then took their own lives. The Park Service calls it the first time enslaved people took control of a colony. [3]

Slavery continued. When Annaberg’s owner James Murphy died in 1808 he held 1,300 acres and 662 enslaved people. After Britain abolished slavery across the strait in 1834, enslaved St. Johnians escaped across the narrow strait — in 1840 eleven fled together to Tortola — until Danish emancipation in 1848. Three rows of foundations from Annaberg’s enslaved laborers’ village survive west of the animal mill. [2]

WAPA.summary:
For the people of Guam, in the words of the park’s brochure, war came early and stayed late. Hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor — December 8, 1941, on Guam’s side of the date line — Japanese planes bombed the U.S. territory, and on December 10 Japanese forces invaded. Under the naval police who ruled the island they renamed Omiyajima, English was forbidden, and Chamorros suspected of hiding Americans or aiding them were beaten, tortured or executed. In 1944 men, women and children were made to work at bayonet point digging shelter caves and building defenses, and in early July 10,000 to 15,000 Chamorros were marched to jungle camps with little food or water; many did not survive. On July 21, 1944, 55,000 U.S. troops landed on the Asan and Agat beaches, and the island was declared secure on August 10, at a cost of over 7,000 American and about 17,500 Japanese casualties. [n]

Congress established War in the Pacific National Historical Park on August 18, 1978. Its seven units, around the villages of Asan, Piti and Agat, keep the invasion beaches, pillboxes, caves and gun emplacements — three Japanese coastal guns at Piti were hauled into place by Chamorros under forced labor — along with the remains of refugee camps where thousands of Chamorros were left homeless. A memorial wall above Asan Bay lists the Americans who died defending and retaking Guam and the people of Guam who suffered and died during 31 months of occupation. More than half the park is coral reef, and the Park Service counts it the most biologically diverse unit in the national park system. [n] [n]

climate.html: The reef fish that were part of the traditional Chamorro diet are still taken for food today, and the reefs are warming. Guam’s shallow reefs bleached every year from 2013 to 2017; heat stress and extreme low tides during the 2014–2015 El Niño ravaged branching Acropora corals on the island’s reef flats, including a site in the park’s Asan unit, and 2017 was the worst year on record for heat stress and bleaching. The Park Service’s 2017 foundation document lists climate change, sea level rise and more intense typhoons among the threats to the park’s reefs and to World War II structures that were hastily built and never meant to last. [n] [n] [n]

indigenous.html:
The Chamorro people, believed to have come from Southeast Asia, raised their houses on stone pillars called latte and were, the 2004 administrative history notes, the only people in Oceania known to have grown rice. Spanish rule brought war and epidemic: in 1671 some 2,000 Chamorros besieged a fortified church for about forty days, and the history estimates that disease and fighting had left about 3,700 people by 1710. [n]

After 1898, the history says, the United States turned over a third of Guam into a military installation and governed through naval officers for most of seventy years; between 1950 and 1952, by Guam government figures, private landholdings fell by more than a quarter as military holdings grew. In 1977 Congress let the District Court of Guam hear claims from families whose land had been taken between 1944 and 1963 without fair condemnation. That resentment, the history concludes, was the setting in which the park was born. [n]

WICA.name: Wind Cave National Park
WICA.summary: Wind Cave National Park in the southern Black Hills of South Dakota protects one of the longest and most complex caves in the world, with over 160 miles of explored passageways, as well as one of the largest remaining mixed-grass prairies in the United States. Wind Cave is distinguished by its extensive boxwork formations — thin calcite fins resembling honeycomb — found in greater quantity here than in any other known cave. The cave is considered sacred by the Lakota people, who know it as "Washun Niya" (the Breathing Hole), and it figures prominently in their creation story as the place from which the Lakota people emerged into the world. Wind Cave was established as the seventh national park in 1903 by President Theodore Roosevelt, making it the first cave to be designated a national park anywhere in the world. The park's surface also supports a free-ranging bison herd descended from animals reintroduced from the Bronx Zoo in 1913.

WRST.summary:
Wrangell-St. Elias is the largest national park in the United States — the brochure counts it as six Yellowstones — a place where four mountain ranges meet and nine of the sixteen highest peaks in the country rise. Mount Wrangell still vents steam near its summit. Near the coast the Bagley Icefield, North America’s largest subpolar icefield, feeds glaciers like the Hubbard and Guyot, and the Malaspina Glacier spills out of the St. Elias Range in a mass larger than Rhode Island. Its more than 9.6 million acres of designated wilderness make up nearly a tenth of the national wilderness system, and with neighboring parks in Canada and Glacier Bay it forms a 24-million-acre World Heritage Site. [1]

This is the homeland of the Ahtna, whose territory takes in the whole Copper River Basin; some 2,500 Ahtna place names — nearly every drainage, hill and ridge named — attest to the length of their presence. Yakutat, on the coast, is a traditional Tlingit fishing village. From 1911 to 1938 the Kennecott mines near McCarthy shipped copper by rail to Cordova, and their ruins are a national historic landmark. President Carter proclaimed the area a national monument on December 1, 1978, and Congress established the 13.2-million-acre park and preserve on December 2, 1980, where local rural residents may still hunt, fish and trap for subsistence. [1] [2]

climate.html: The Tlingit named the Malaspina Glacier Sít’ Tlein, Big Glacier. At about 2,400 square kilometres it is the world’s largest piedmont glacier, and it is thinning by more than a metre a year. A 2023 radar-mapping study found that two-thirds of it is grounded below sea level, its bed cut by channels that reach more than 350 metres below sea level, and that only a narrow, eroding strip of ice-cored land separates it from the Gulf of Alaska — where lagoons have formed in front of the glacier in recent decades. If the sea breaks through, the authors warn, retreat could be rapid, and the glacier holds enough ice to raise global sea level by 1.4 millimetres. [4]

sources.title: Tober et al., Comprehensive Radar Mapping of Malaspina Glacier (Sít' Tlein), Alaska, Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface 128 (2023)

indigenous.html: The Copper River, called ’Atna’ or “beyond river” in Ahtna, runs 290 miles from the Wrangells to the Gulf of Alaska, and the Ahtna have worked and traded its copper for centuries — archeologists think for 500 to 1,000 years. In 1885 Chief Nicolai showed Lt. Henry Allen a copper vein, and later revealed a source to prospectors for a cache of supplies. Some writers demeaned him as an innocent who traded a multimillion-dollar mine for food; Pratt (1998), as summarized in the 2024 ethnographic overview, argued instead that he was canny in his dealings and that his death in 1899 or 1900 opened the floodgates to rapid outside exploitation. Simeone and Miller call the Kennecott mine one of the grandest colonial land thefts in early twentieth-century Alaska: the Ahtna received no compensation for the land or the ore, though they could ride the railroad free. Ahtna reaction to the 1978 monument, the authors write, was mixed: many supported protection for the lands their subsistence depended on, but Alaska Native people felt their voices were sidelined at points in the debates over land selections and protected areas. [2]

sources.title: Simeone & Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS, 2024)

labor_ccc.html: At Kennecott, a 14-story concentrator stepped down the hillside so gravity could carry ore through the mill. In 1916 the mines produced 101,410,000 pounds of copper; William Douglass, later Kennecott’s superintendent, reckoned it achieved a third of the Anaconda mine’s production in Butte with only 500 workers to Anaconda’s 15,000. The mill town was ordered by rank, the manager’s house and staff quarters at its center; the bunkhouses had no facilities for families, so married miners usually left theirs behind. In June 1917 miners struck — the only strike at Kennecott — for a flat wage instead of one that slid with copper prices. In arbitration 45 days later the company kept its sliding scale but granted a 50-cent daily raise and a new bunkhouse, mess hall and recreation hall at the Bonanza Mine; it refused collective contracts and rehired only one member of the Miners Committee. [3]

sources.title: Cultural Landscape Report: Kennecott Mill Town, Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve (NPS, 2001), Part I Site History

women.html: Two Ahtna elders, Katie John and Doris Charles, pushed the federal government into managing subsistence fishing across much of Alaska. In 1983 they and the Mentasta Village Council asked the state to let them fish at Tanada Creek, which the state had closed to fishing in 1964; at Batzulnetas, their natal village, salmon had been taken for hundreds of years. Refused, they sued. In March 1994 a federal court ruled that the federal government could manage subsistence fisheries on navigable waters, and the ruling was upheld in April 1995. Thousands marched in Anchorage in their support, Rosa Parks among them. John said she fought so her grandchildren would remember the way she had learned. Their victory opened Batzulnetas and extended federal subsistence jurisdiction to more than half of Alaska’s navigable waters. [2]

sources.title: Simeone & Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS, 2024)

YOSE.summary:
Yosemite covers 747,956 acres of the central Sierra Nevada: granite domes and cliffs, waterfalls, three groves of giant sequoias, alpine meadows and the headwaters of the Tuolumne and Merced rivers, which supply drinking water to millions of people in the San Francisco Bay Area. About a million years ago glaciers moved down the river valleys — ice in Yosemite Valley may have been 4,000 feet thick — and carved the U-shaped valley visitors know today. More than 94 percent of the park is designated wilderness. [2]

Oral tradition and archeological evidence, the Park Service’s 2016 foundation document says, suggest people have lived continuously in the Yosemite region for at least 8,000 years, and seven present-day tribes descend from those who first called it home. On June 30, 1864, President Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, giving Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove to California to be held for public use, resort and recreation, inalienable for all time — the first scenic natural area set aside by the United States for public benefit. Congress created the surrounding national park on October 1, 1890; California returned the valley and the grove in 1905 and Congress accepted them in 1906. [2] [1]

More than four million people a year now enter the park. Its own documents describe a landscape still being remade — by rockfall and flood, by fire after a century of protecting the sequoias from it, and by a warming climate pushing the pika upslope — and a human history that includes the 1851 militia campaign against the valley’s Ahwahneechee people. [2] [1] [3]

black.html: From 1891 to 1914, before the Park Service existed, the U.S. Army guarded Yosemite and the other Sierra parks. In 1899 the 24th Infantry patrolled the backcountry, and the 9th Cavalry followed in 1903 and 1904 — both regiments of African American soldiers, the Buffalo Soldiers, formed after the Civil War. Shelton Johnson argues that the nearly 500 soldiers who served over those three years were long left out of the park’s histories; Carl Russell’s One Hundred Years in Yosemite never names either regiment. He calls them invisible men and contends that such gaps in history are made, not accidental. The Park Service’s 2016 foundation document now names the Army’s role, including the Buffalo Soldiers, in its statement of the park’s significance. [4] [2]

sources.title: Johnson, Invisible Men: Buffalo Soldiers of the Sierra Nevada (NPS Yosemite, undated), pp. 1–6
Foundation Document, Yosemite National Park (NPS, 2016), significance statement 12

climate.html: The 2019 park brochure points to the pika, a small, heat-intolerant animal of the high-country rock piles, whose habitat is shifting upward as the climate rapidly warms — and asks where pikas will go when they run out of mountain. The 2016 foundation document names climate change a key issue: drought had already killed large numbers of ponderosa pines and other trees at lower elevations, and less snowpack and earlier runoff could bring longer, drier summers, larger and more intense wildfires and more flooding as precipitation falls as rain. The park is restoring meadows, riverbanks and the Mariposa Grove and using prescribed and managed fire; the brochure notes that a century of protecting sequoias from fire had harmed the trees it meant to save. [1] [2]

indigenous.html:
The Ahwahneechee, a Southern Sierra Miwok tribelet, lived in and around the valley they called Ahwahnee. Gold Rush miners and settlers burned their villages and felled oak groves; Indians had no civil or legal rights. Governor John McDougal — who, Greene writes, had once spoken to the legislature of the inevitability of the extermination of the Indian race — authorized a militia: the 200-man Mariposa Battalion under trader James Savage, mustered in January 1851. Savage threatened to annihilate Chief Tenaya’s people if they resisted, then burned their dwellings and food caches to starve them onto reservations. In May another company shot two captives trying to escape; one was Tenaya’s youngest son. [3]

In June 1852 Army troops shot five Indians found with clothing suspected to be the murdered prospectors’. In 1907 the Army took Koomine, the valley’s largest village, as a camp and forced out its residents; in 1969 the Park Service moved the last family from its 1933 Indian Village and burned it. [3]

sources.title: Greene, Historic Resource Study, Vol. 1 (NPS, 1987), ch. I, sections A, C–E (pp. 1–28)

labor_ccc.html: Ten Civilian Conservation Corps camps operated in Yosemite between May 1933 and October 1940, with 6,816 enrollees assigned — unemployed, unmarried young men of 18 to 25 typically earning thirty dollars a month, twenty-five of which went home to their families. Each camp held 225 to 250 men, mostly from cities, alongside local recruits and experienced local men. They built log curbing and paths around Yosemite Village, revived the 250 apple trees settler James Lamon had planted, and replaced the posts of the Half Dome cable route, drilling 41 holes into the rock by hand while roped to the posts. The Cascades camp on Highway 140 was wiped out in the 1937 flood. [6]

sources.title: Orr, The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) in Yosemite, Yosemite (Yosemite Association), Vol. 67 No. 4, Fall 2005, pp. 2–4

women.html: Enid Michael, a third-grade teacher from Pasadena, moved to the park in May 1919 and became one of the four members of Yosemite’s first Nature Guide Service. She published 195 articles in Yosemite Nature Notes and from 1931 directed the planting of a wildflower garden behind the Yosemite Museum, funded by a $4,000 gift from Marjorie Montgomery Ward, that came to hold more than a thousand plants. Some male colleagues resented a woman in the job: in 1923 she rallied the California Federation of Women’s Clubs to press for a permanent appointment, and a handwritten note on a 1937 memo said Civilian Conservation Corps boys should work under a male naturalist, the word underlined four times. After twenty-one seasonal reappointments, her service ended on September 30, 1942. [5]

sources.title: Peñalosa, Enid Michael: Yosemite’s First Woman Ranger-Naturalist, Yosemite (Yosemite Association), Vol. 66 No. 3, Summer 2004, pp. 3–6
